title: 'Mind-blowing' - Lachlan Morton's mid-point assessment of Pony Express endurance ride across 'very desolate landscapes' of US western states
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
Lachlan Morton passed the midway point Thursday on his latest long-distance challenge, the Pony Express route , camping for a few hours in Wyoming with rugged terrain populated by sagebrush and occasional cattle. Before his reprieve ahead on day four, riding through Utah's Emigration Canyon into Salt Lake City, the Australian gave an update to .

The ride so far, he said, was living up to expectations of "remote and harsh". He started on Monday in St. Joseph, Missouri, for the 3,164-kilometre (1,966-mile) ride across eight US western states into Sacramento, California. The route was made famous in the early 1860s by mail carriers racing on horseback. Morton is retracing the almost-exact path, using pedal power.

"I mean, there's just very desolate landscapes. They're all very different and challenging in their own way, but they're all very remote and harsh," he said in recorded answers to questions sent by of his first impressions of the route through Kansas, Nebraska, a touch into Colorado, and into Wyoming.

"I'm familiar with these landscapes, but then piecing them all together in this way, it's pretty mind-blowing."

At this point Morton was on the rough, almost-forgotten double-track leading from Wyoming to Salt Lake City. He had already encountered herds of cattle passing precariously close across his path and had a re-route through deep sand and leg-scratching brush under dark Wyoming skies when the almost-forgotten path seemed to vanish.

The original pioneers who raced across the open prairies and treacherous mountains switched their mounts several times to deliver papers and messages in eight days or less. The record on horseback was set in 1861 at seven days, 17 hours. Morton looks to beat that record, meeting up with support to switch bikes. It is a proper way for him to make his final ride in EF Education-EasyPost colours and equipment, where he has raced in multiple disciplines for 12 of the last 16 seasons.

"It's using all the different bikes I've ridden, and it's also very much a team effort. This is not something I could do by myself. It's relying on a group of people that I've come to know through my time with EF, and it's very much requiring a big effort by all of us, which I think has kind of been the story of my time with the team," he said.

The team posted to social media on Thursday that he was ahead of schedule, with a "400-kilometre lead over the Pony Express' fastest time" in Utah. However, the toughest terrain approached, and he admitted the opening days gave him a better understanding of the difficulty of the journey 160 years ago.

"I think it's a super interesting story for Pony Express, and the fact that it was around such a short time and is still, somehow, very celebrated and well known today," he said, referring to the two-year span of the Pony Express before the telegraph replaced the physical delivery of important messages.

"Seeing these landscapes and even trying to imagine doing it on horseback at all times in a year, night and day, it's pretty mind-blowing. I'm realising, I think, the power of the route."

On the weekend he'll cross Nevada, heading south of Lake Tahoe when he crosses the Sierra Nevada mountains that mark entry into California. In the true spirit of the route, Morton will deliver letters. It's all a flashback into history made real.

"It wasn't that there was heaps of people suddenly delivering mail. Ultimately, it didn't really work, it was never profitable. But the power of it was exciting. You know, it was something for people to be excited about at a time when the country was going through crazy change, and a lot of conflict. This was just a human-powered effort in a way that could get people excited about the country.

"That's kind of why I like to do these things. It's fun to do, but it's also nice to see people have something to follow for the sake of following and be excited about."

The names of the adventurous riders who blazed the first trails west are forever remembered on a Pony Express National Museum website . Perhaps Morton can make the list, with an asterisk. Follow Morton's progress online .

title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Joe Pepitone
author: Matt Ferenchick
text:
Happy birthday to a hero of a Yankees’ down period.

The period between the 1964 World Series loss and the return to the Fall Classic in 1976 is a bit of a wasteland in Yankees’ history. Thanks in large part to the disaster that was CBS ownership, the Yankees had some of their worst years during that time. Things started to turn around by the start of the 1970s, as young players like Thurman Munson began to develop.

However, it’s not as if the Yankees had no good players in that down era. It’s not as if the children following the team didn’t have their idols. One of them is Joe Pepitone, whose birthday we celebrate today.

Joseph Anthony “Joe” Pepitone Born: October 9, 1940 (Brooklyn, NY) Died: March 13, 2023 (Kansas City, MO) Yankees Tenure: 1962-69

Joe Pepitone was born on October 9, 1940, in the very city he would go on play in professionally. The oldest of three boys, he grew up in Brooklyn with his parents Willie and Angelina. Although Joe said he loved and admired his father, the elder Pepitone could be abusive, both physically and emotionally. In one particular incident, Joe telling his father “I hate you!” caused Willie to hurl an ash tray in the direction of his son. It didn’t hit Joe, but it smashed against the wall, causing shards to fly in his eyes. There was no permanent damage, but the physical abuse did end after that harrowing incident. His father passed away in 1958, just a day after Joe had told his mom that “I wish he’d die” after another blowup between the two of them.

Pepitone was introduced to baseball by an uncle, and honed his game playing in the sandlots of New York City. A star in high school at Manual Training High School (now John Jay High School), Pepitone also played for Nathan’s Hot Dog semipro team when he began to catch the eyes of scouts. However, he had another nearly life-altering incident before he began his professional career.

In March 1958, just weeks before Pepitone would begin in minor league career, he was shot in an incident at his high school. A classmate had found a gun on the docks, and had pointed it — possibly, hopefully jokingly — at Pepitone, who didn’t know what was happening, tried backing away. The gun accidentally went off, and Pepitone had been shot straight through the stomach. Thankfully, Pepitone somehow escaped mostly uninjured, and signed for the Yankees shortly after that.

After signing with the Yankees, Pepitone rocketed through the minor leauges, and made the majors after impressing following a spring training with the big league team in 1962. Early on, Pepitone’s playing time was sparse with Bill “Moose” Skowron entrenched as the Yankees’ first baseman. As the calendar turned to May, manager Ralph Houk began to use him more, often deploying him in the outfield. However, after struggles and a disciplinary incident, the Yankees sent the youngster back down to the minors. He put up big numbers there and got called back up, although he wouldn’t appear in the 1962 World Series, which would be the Yankees’ last Fall Classic victory until 1977.

The 1963 season would go on to be a breakthrough one for Pepitone. He slugged 27 home runs and was named an All-Star, starting the game at first base. Pepitone would end up making the All-Star team in 1964 and ‘65 as well, along with helping the Yankees to the 1963 and ‘64 AL pennants. They lost both those series, though and Pepitone would never appear in the postseason again.

Over the next couple years, Pepitone became a star for the Yankees. However, with the stars of the 1950s and early 60s dynasty aging out, the team began to go the wrong way in the standings. With a career 105 OPS+ while on the Yankees, Pepitone was hardly ever the problem on the field. However, he could often be a bit of one off it. He gained the reputation as a bit of a party boy and had a habit of showing up late and having disagreements with managers. Between that and the fact that he was one of the higher earners on a bad Yankees’ team, the decision was eventually made to trade him. In December 1969, he was sent to the Astros for Curt Blefary.

Pepitone had a couple stops after his Yankee career, most notably with the Cubs from 1970-73. After his MLB career ended, he had a brief stint with the Yakult Atoms in Japan. He eventually returned to the Bronx as a coach, and was credited with helping Don Mattingly master first base defensively. However, his off-field issues remained, and he even did prison time after a 1988 drug conviction. He later released a fairly candid autobiography, where he spoke at length about his issues, and how they led to the end of three marriages and kept him from being an even better player.

In later years, Pepitone became something of a pop culture reference point. He was mentioned on occasions on “Seinfield” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” with noted Yankee fan Larry David right in the age range to remember Pepitone’s peak.

He was also the subject of a mention in a flashback scene in “The Sopranos.”

In his later years, Pepitone settled in Kansas City, where he was living with one of his children. He often made time to return to Yankees alumni events though, including Old-Timers’ Day in the Bronx. Pepitone passed away in KC at the age of 82 in 2023.

Nobody will mistake Joe Pepitone for a Baseball Hall of Famer, his stats weren’t remotely there. However, for Yankees’ fans of the time, watching a local kid make good, you couldn’t have told them otherwise.

title: Tiffany Cromwell, Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio Call It a Career at UCI Gravel Worlds after 17-Years in the Peloton
author: sstokes
text:
Tiffany Cromwell pictured at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race with her partner, Formula One driver Valtteri Bottas (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @Dario Belingheri/@Getty Images)

Two standout racers are set to hang up their wheels this weekend, ending their professional careers at the UCI Gravel Worlds in Nannup, Western Australia.

Both Tiffany Cromwell and Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio are saying goodbye after 17 seasons in the pro peloton.

They both began with the Lotto Ladies team in 2010, spending two seasons there, before branching out in different directions.

Their careers will converge one last time at the UCI Gravel Worlds this weekend in what will be an emotional weekend.

“I’ve been fortunate to have had a very long cycling career with only one major injury,” Cromwell said recently on social media. “I’ve also been able to experience and be a part of the massive change and growth of women’s cycling.

“There’s been many highs and lows and many amazing memories. And I’m happy to be able to finish on my own terms.”

The 38-year-old has had a high public profile within the sport, winning the women’s Omloop Het Nieuwsblad in 2013 plus stages of the Giro d’Italia Internazionale Femminile in 2012 and 2016.

More recently she has been dividing her time between road and gravel, winning the European championships in the latter in 2023, and also taking victories in UCI Gravel World Series races including Sea Otter Europe in 2024.

She won the Unbound Gravel 100 last year.

Over the past decade and a half she has seen huge changes in the sport, and will depart with women’s cycling in far better condition than when she started.

“I’ve been fortunate to ride this wave of women’s cycling. When we started, it was for the love of it,” the Australian told SBS. “There was limited support, the money wasn’t there. To have a career, the longevity wasn’t there.

“And then seeing the sport grow, seeing events globally pick up, seeing new disciplines like gravel come in and having the opportunity to race that and to follow the wave of gravel as well and the growth…I am very fortunate because I can appreciate where the sport has come from and where it is now, versus those coming into the sport now… They are in a lot better position but they don’t understand the demands are higher, the level is higher, the stress, everything is higher.”

Cromwell is the partner of F1 driver Valtteri Bottas, making them a pro athlete power couple of sorts.

He recently supported her at the Philadelphia Cycling Cassic, handing up bottles as the Canyon SRAM rider helped teammate Chiara Consonni to victory.

Bottas recorded a chat with Cromwell before that race, asking what her main feeling was as the end of her carer drew closer.

“I don’t have to hurt myself any more,” she said, smiling. “Except for three more times [on gravel].”

“Except when you go riding with me,” he replied.

“Then you will need to wait for me … I will need an e-bike,” she quipped.

Cromwell described the Philly event as a great one to close out the road chapter of her career. “An iconic race with so much history that was back for the first time in 10 years,” she wrote.

“The atmosphere was electric and as an added bonus we managed to take home the victory as a team with @chiara_consonnii.”

Consonnii is 11 years her junior and is one of those younger riders she said faced an environment with more opportunities than before, but also much greater demands.

Cromwell takes satisfaction in seeing this evolution take place.

“It’s been cool to watch,” she told SBS. “It is great to see that women’s cycling is finally getting to a place it deserves to be and I am sure it is going to grow in the years to come.

“I can look back and kind of talk about the old stories of what we used to have to where we are now and having the opportunity to race in races like the Tour de France avec Zwift and big gravel races, world championships, big races around the world.”

Moolman-Pasio has also competed in the biggest events and while her online exposure is less than that of the media-savvy Cromwell, she had an even bigger career.

The South African clocked up 49 wins on the road, including a Giro stage in 2021, and was second overall in the race in 2018 and 2021. GC victories include the Tour de Romandie Féminin and Emakumeen Bira.

She has been a trailblazer for African sport and will take over as general manager of Team Amani next year. The team is aiming to compete in the 2028 Tour and her experience will be invaluable in moving it towards that goal.

This weekend, though, her mind is on the worlds.

“One more time on the start line as a pro,” she wrote on Friday.

“Tomorrow is officially my last race as a professional cyclist at the Gravel World Champs in Nannup, Australia. I’d hoped to arrive feeling my best, but unfortunately I’ve come down with a head cold.

“It’s disappointing, especially because I’ve been feeling strong and I really like the course here in Nannup. But the doctor has confirmed it’s not in my chest, so I’ll be starting and seeing what the day brings. I hope to enjoy these final race kilometres and soak it all in.”

Cromwell, too, will share those sentiments. It’s a very exciting time for both, in terms of future opportunities, but also an emotional one as the final days, hours and minutes of their careers tick down.

title: 'World Championships were just a snapshot' – Back to full confidence, Remco Evenepoel says victory at Il Lombardia would make 2026 his 'best season yet'
author: James Moultrie
text:
Six years after his horror crash at Il Lombardia, Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) is looking to close that chapter fully and cap off what would be "the best season of his career" with a maiden victory at the final Monument in 2026.

Speaking at a press conference on Friday, Evenepoel reportedly brought up the incident himself, which saw him crash over a bridge wall into a ravine on he steep descent off the Colma di Sormano.

While insisting it won't play on his mind during the race, especially as the climb is not included on this year's route to Como, Evenepoel did speak about how that crash will always make recons on the same roads in Lombardy special to him.

"It was good to check out the finale with the Civiglio, because I've never done that climb in a race before. In 2020 I didn't make it there because of that crash," he said, as reported by Flemish broadcaster .

"Because of the past, this race will always be special to me. During my reconnaissance, I passed by the hospital where I was treated 6 years ago [having fractured his pelvis and suffered a lung contusion in the crash].

"But none of that is on my mind. A victory could make it feel completely different, yes. Then we could wrap up the story and close the book. But it won't freeze me in this final."

Without five-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar taking the start, out injured, Evenepoel will start as one of the heavy favourites alongside Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM), and Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek). At 239km and with just under 5,000m of elevation gain, the Belgian believes the route should fit into his wheelhouse.

"It will be special with a difficult start featuring a few long climbs. Then follow two long valleys and short climbs at the end. So it seems like you get two races with an explosive finale at the end. That should suit me," he said, adding quiet confidence after identifying his main rivals.

"Seixas and Del Toro are obviously on fire, but there are more guys like Ciccone, Matteo Jorgenson and Tom Pidcock. Jarno Widar also looked good this week, but this is a different story altogether, with a lot of positioning work and many descents. That is something new for him.

"So you can't give very many guys 5 stars. If it can only be for one rider? Then go for me. But it will be an open race compared to previous years where the same rider won every time."

But after winning the European Championships road race last weekend, and with some reassurance from his entourage, the confidence has returned in time for the big appointment. He's been second at Lombardia twice, both behind Pogačar in 2025 and 2024, and will be desperate to go one better and add to his two Monument titles from Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

"After the World Championships, there was a sort of doubt as to whether I would get back into good form, but my trainer, team manager, and those back home reminded me that my World Championship time trial had still been super good," said Evenepoel.

"If you don't perform as you hope on the day of the appointment, you start to have some doubts. And you think: maybe it won't work out at the end of the year? But last Thursday I was able to train well towards the European Championships, and then I realized that the World Championships had been a snapshot.

"That European title gave me extra motivation. In any case, I can get over a disappointment quickly and refocus, but it certainly helped me."

In August last year, it was announced that Evenepoel would be breaking his Soudal-QuickStep contract early to join Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe in 2026. Fast forward to October, and with two stage wins and second overall at the Tour de France, victories at Amstel Gold Race, GP de Québec and Clasicá San Sebastián, podium finishes at Liège and the Tour of Flanders, and 13 wins in total, including a fourth consecutive ITT world title and the European road title , it's been nothing short of a major success.

"It's been pretty good. The classics campaign was pretty good, but I didn't necessarily reach the level I wanted. After Catalonia and my crash, it might have given a distorted picture, but I have been in better form in April," he said.

"Despite the good results, that was a somewhat weaker moment, but a strong summer followed. I have taken a step forward. Especially in the Grand Tours. That motivates us for the future.

"This is definitely one of my better seasons. If I win on Saturday, this will be my best season yet. Especially with my strong Tour. It would be a nice way to finish."

title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
author: Julian Borger and Rachel Savage
text:
Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza .

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X , adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement , the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize , the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa , home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.…

title: Burnham promises to curb non-compete rules in job contracts
text:
Andy Burnham has promised to curb companies' ability to restrict what their workers can do after leaving their job.

In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back.

He added the clauses had forced workers to go without pay after leaving a role, as well as making it harder for growing firms to hire new staff.

Ahead of the Budget later this month, he also said there was "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had been exploring possible restrictions on non-compete clauses since late last year, including a total ban, banning them above a certain salary threshold, or limiting how long they can last.

Although commonly associated with the financial services and technology sectors, research cited by the government has estimated around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by the clauses, typically lasting around six months.

Speaking at a business summit in Manchester, Burnham confirmed his government would press ahead with new legislation to ensure the clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring new staff.

He added that their use had stopped workers leaving to join other companies, or founding their own firms instead, adding: "I think that's a drag on innovation."

Referencing a landmark 1995 court ruling that is credited with revolutionising the football transfer market in Europe, he said he hoped reining in non-compete clauses could prove the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector".

Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms".

It is understood that the government is planning to unveil details of the proposed restrictions, which were first reported by Politico , external and The Financial Times , external , alongside the Budget on 28 October.

Responding to the prime minister's comments, the Recruitment and Employment Confederation warned against "sweeping" changes to non-compete rules, adding they played a "vital role" in protecting commercially sensitive information and client relationships.

The previous Conservative government had ruled out a total ban , external on non-compete clauses, after hearing from employers that it could reduce investor confidence in the UK or prompt companies to tighten how they share information internally.

The prime minister sought to frame the announcement on non-compete clauses as part of a wider government pitch to boost innovative sectors of the economy.

He told the summit that although the UK was home to outstanding research and start-ups, too many companies had gone abroad in search of investment.

He also signalled that the government would "say more" at the Budget about plans to use public investment as a way to encourage private funding in the economy.

He added that he wanted all UK regions to have a dedicated fund to do this, modelled on the Good Growth Fund launched in Greater Manchester last year, during his tenure as mayor of the city-region.

He also hinted that the government was looking at the tax system to ensure the UK can retain high-growth companies.

He said: "One of our biggest challenges is breaking through our own ceiling. Too often, our best ideas are developed and scaled overseas, and with it the jobs, technology and investment that goes with them."

"So I know there is more to do to fix that, specifically on tax, to encourage people to stay and scale."

title: Ex-Deutsche Bank trader has conviction for rigging interest rates quashed
author: Joanna Partridge
text:
Former City banker becomes eighth to clear their name, just days after five others were acquitted

Former City trader Christian Bittar has become the eighth person to have his conviction for rigging interest rates quashed, just days after five other former bankers also successfully cleared their names .

Christian Bittar, who previously worked for Deutsche Bank, was convicted in 2018 of conspiracy to defraud.

On Wednesday, the court overturned the convictions of Jay Vijay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham, all of whom worked at Barclays .

This week’s acquittals come just over a year after the UK supreme court overturned a decade-old ruling against the former UBS and Citigroup trader Tom Hayes and former Barclays trader Carlo Palombo. Their victory opened the door for the other traders to challenge their convictions.

Bittar said after his acquittal: “I have waited a very, very long time for this day. Finally, the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised. I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it.”

Bittar and the five other former traders were all sentenced to jail on charges of manipulating the euro interbank offered rate (Euribor) or the now defunct London interbank offered rate (Libor).

The Euribor and Libor rates affected the value of ordinary people’s pensions, mortgages and savings, as well as hundreds of trillions of pounds and euros worth of financial products around the world. Nine bankers accused of rigging the rates were given fraud convictions.

The supreme court overturned the convictions of Hayes and Palombo after finding faults in the original trials, ruling that trial judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” instructions to the juries, that had ultimately “deprived” the men a fair trial.

Friday’s ruling marks a further blow for the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original charges against the former traders.

While the SFO did not contest the appeals of the five men acquitted on Wednesday, it did contest Bittar’s appeal, stating his conviction was safe.

Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO, said: “ We argued for a different outcome but respect the court’s decision in relation to Christian Bittar. The SFO remains committed to tackling the most complex fraud, bribery and corruption.”

Ben Rose of law firm Hickman and Rose, who represented Bittar, said it was a “scandal that the SFO has consistently failed to uphold its duty to ensure that these trials are fair”.

Peter Johnson, the ninth former trader who was convicted of rate rigging, also intends to appeal against his conviction. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to manipulate Libor in 2014.

Ellen Gallagher, a partner at Vardags, who represents Johnson, said: “Peter’s fight to clear his name continues.

“As the court made clear today, he has taken the first steps towards that appeal by filing provisional grounds.”

title: Verstappen on sprint pole after another settings issue
text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen beat Mercedes driver George Russell to sprint pole at the Singapore Grand Prix.

Verstappen, fresh from his and Red Bull's first victory of the season in Malaysia last weekend, was 0.12 seconds quicker than the Briton, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc third.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were fourth and fifth ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who went early in final qualifying and fell down the order from initially being second behind Leclerc.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli, using the Mercedes upgrade that underperformed in Malaysia while Russell is on the previous specification, could manage only seventh.

And there were further glitches with the engine settings provided by governing body the FIA five days after the formation laps in the wet in Malaysia saw cars reduced to crawling speed as a result of a software bug.

Mercedes critics think I'm Satan - Wolff

The settings issue in Singapore, which was combined with a glitch in the F1 timing system that delayed the start of second qualifying, affected all cars but had a bigger impact on some drivers than others, depending on the timing of their runs.

The problem involved the settings being different before and after a red flag caused by a crash for Sergio Perez's Cadillac and left drivers complaining of reduced power.

It involved overtake mode - which allows an extra 0.5MJ of energy to be harvested - being switched on and off again in the space of 28 seconds.

Williams driver Carlos Sainz was knocked out in the first session after what we described as a "really poor lap", but added: "On top of that, half the cars did the lap with half a second quicker engine than the others.

"There was another software issue and we were on the bad end of it, and for whatever reason, the FIA, like in Malaysia, again didn't decide to do sporting equity and were happy to do half of the quali with cars with higher power than the other half of the cars.

"A bit confused why the sport keeps doing different things depending on who is out in Q1 or who is out in lap one."

Sainz said he did not think he would have made it through even without the settings problem.

Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll were other drivers who were affected and were knocked out in the first session. Stroll's team-mate Fernando Alonso also suffered, but did progress, eventually qualifying 15th.

The FIA said in a statement: "During the first period of sprint qualifying there was a human error in race control unrelated to the timing issue also encountered in SQ1.

"This issue in question meant overtake mode was not available after the red flag period during SQ1.

"When it became apparent that overtake mode was not active after the restart, it was then activated for a period of 27 seconds before being deactivated again.

"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap.

"The second and third periods of sprint qualifying were not affected."

The FIA system automatically disables overtake mode when there is a red flag. A pop-up then appears on the screen asking whether officials want to re-enable it.

This was ignored, then overtake mode was reactivated before being disabled again, on the basis that it was fairer to do so than leave it enabled.

Verstappen's pole lap appeared to be further confirmation of Red Bull's resurgence after his dominant win in Malaysia.

He faced an investigation for overtaking Hamilton under yellow flags shown before the first session was stopped for the Perez incident, but officials took no further action.

The four-time champion said he had not believed pole was possible before qualifying.

"We have some difficulties with the car in ride, as we know," he said, "but at least when we went to the soft tyres (in the final session), it made the car a bit more stable in places where before you were a bit unsure.

"I did not expect this but you take it, I'm happy for sure. Qualifying tomorrow is still the main goal and for us the start is always a critical point but at least a positive end to our day."

Russell's performance compared with that of Antonelli raises further doubts about the efficacy of the Mercedes upgrade introduced in Malaysia.

It was their biggest car update since the Canadian Grand Prix in May but team boss Toto Wolff said at Sepang that it had appeared to take them backwards rather than forwards.

Mercedes split the car spec here in Singapore in an attempt to better understand its performance but Antonelli ended the session 0.573secs behind Russell.

The Briton said: "As a team there is still nothing telling us it isn't working but it's all driven by the stopwatch and, yeah, the stopwatch hasn't been great for the upgrade yet. Maybe tomorrow's a different day."

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

Antonelli, who leads the championship by 84 points going into the weekend, said: "Already FP1 I was struggling and there is still a lot to understand about this package. Really the car is very difficult, very unpredictable, very difficult to put a lap together. It's a shame. I was coming with high hopes but so far it has been very difficult.

"It's going to be a difficult weekend unless we can pull something out tomorrow. Other than that it is going very tricky. I don't really see where we can find 0.7secs but you never know."

Wolff said before sprint qualifying: "The new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive. Not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it. The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point."

Leclerc was 0.243secs off pole, and ruing what he said was Ferrari "losing a little bit of our raw performance" in the past three or four races.…

title: Manchester United’s early wobble makes Tottenham visit a must-win for Carrick
author: Will Unwin
text:
After a scratchy start in the league, injuries and an underwhelming Rashford, Spurs’s visit to Old Trafford is already crucial for the hosts

T he noise in the Premier League was focused elsewhere for the last two weeks of the international break, allowing a glorious silence to drift across Manchester United. Without Manchester City’s woes , Michael Carrick may have faced a more difficult time, with plenty to review in regards to the first five games of the season.

United sit solemnly in 12th with only one league win, and misery needs company. The hosts will find just that at Old Trafford on Saturday evening. Tottenham, bottom of the Premier League, visit, with both sides hoping to kickstart their season. Spurs have secured a measly two points after a summer where £300m was spent on Roberto De Zerbi’s rebuild but the architect’s drawings are already at risk of being set alight. For Carrick and United, beating the worst team in the league is close to a necessity as they enter a very difficult run of fixtures.

October is theoretically and practically problematic for United, who have six fixtures this month, with away games against Leeds, Atlético Madrid, Como and Chelsea, who play a variety of styles that need preparing for, making a home game against Spurs a must-win. On paper, the second easiest game of the month is Bournemouth at home. Carrick has plenty of credit in the bank from his work in the second half of last season, and will be afforded as much time as possible to get things right because no one is eager for another mid-season change of manager. United need to be in a better position by the end of October than they started it, which will require significant improvement on the pitch.

For Carrick there are plenty of small margins he can point to. The opening-day defeat at Hull was a grisly performance and worthy of criticism; Ipswich were eventually dispatched, while the derby was a tight and controversial loss , coming between two draws. The truth of the matter is United know they need to be better in both boxes. United have conceded fewer opposition touches in their box than any other team in the league but, on the other hand, they are the only side yet to keep a clean sheet. They can also boast the most touches in opposition boxes but are largely incapable of killing matches off.

United, like Tottenham, are very good at dominating possession, averaging 60% per match, but cannot translate that to goals and points. Even in the victory against Ipswich, United were unable to put a full 90 minutes of composure together, relying on Bruno Fernandes to drag them through against a promoted side. The forwards are yet to synchronise, with Matheus Cunha, the man tasked with leading the line, having only one goal to his name, and even that took a heavy deflection.

No one has more than one assist so far, while only Fernandes and Bryan Mbeumo have scored twice or more, the Portuguese getting a hat-trick against Ipswich. Marcus Rashford has shown glimpses of promise on the left but has no goal involvements, giving the impression of a man who requires a confidence boost after returning to the club where he was not wanted for 18 months. Nor is there the option of Benjamin Sesko playing as a more traditional central striker given he is sidelined with injury, while Joshua Zirkzee cannot even class himself as a plan B. But United are prolific compared with Tottenham, whose only league goals came in a 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa just before the international break.

Losing to 10-man Manchester City was the most worrying of United’s defeats, showing how far off they look against a Champions League side. Phil Foden’s red card gave United plenty of space but they were unable to take advantage, instead plodding around, short of ideas, barely threatening. United are expert at dominating possession but not games, traits that create hope and frustration in equal measure.

The summer signings of a goalkeeper who cost nothing and three central midfielders is coming under as much scrutiny as Carrick’s tactics. At least Carlos Baleba is poised to finally make his debut after joining from Brighton for £65m in August and Carrick desperately needs him to provide the energy lacking in central areas thus far. Having recovered from an ankle injury, the Cameroonian has what it takes to snuff out the danger that has been leading to the concession of goals.

Sesko is not the sole injury concern; Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford were ruled out of playing for England, while Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui’s international breaks ended prematurely. Meanwhile, Matthijs de Ligt has not played competitively for 10 months and Amad Diallo is yet to feature this season.

The run of 12 wins in 17 games after Carrick took interim charge in January showed plenty of individual and collective improvements, but whether certain players can crash through their current ceiling requires clear evidence sooner rather than later. With finances tight, it is imperative that United improve from within. More academy players have spent time with the squad in recent weeks, with Noah Ajayi impressing the coaches Steve Holland and Jonathan Woodgate. It is thought a number of youngsters could make first-team debuts before the season concludes, which would be a display of Carrick’s long-term vision. Results, however, will decide if he gets a chance to implement it in the first place.

United are desperate for a catalyst and if it does not come against Tottenham at the weekend, Carrick will become fearful of Halloween.

title: China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal
author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
text:
Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs

The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.

Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.

The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.

“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.

China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.

Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.

He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.

“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.

“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart.

Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.

Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.

As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.

China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.

The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.

A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.

It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.

While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

title: Cycling is Cheap, $6,500 Wheels, and the Mistakes We Remember Making | Velo Podcast
author: Josh Ross
text:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

This week, Lisa Charlebois, our host Mike Levy, and I (Josh Ross) will be riding in Death Valley when you hear this. With that in mind, we had a discussion—including Logan Jones-Wilkins who will only be on the ride in spirit—all about the mistakes we’ve made.

It starts with Logan giving me a bit of a hard time. The problem is that I’m so risk-averse I don’t actually have a ton of examples. If left to my own devices, I tend to move slowly and plan things carefully to avoid disaster. Mistakes do happen though, and I have a few. Lisa has a few more, and Logan has a few more too. Pretty soon though, this just devolves into the Levy show. Mike is far from risk-averse, and the number of things he’s done with his body moving faster than his ability to contemplate the results is pretty extensive.

We do have some other things to chat about this week before we get into all the Mike Levy disasters, though. Did you know that laces are more aerodynamic than BOA dials? Logan noticed a lot of riders at Worlds seemed to be into laces, so he jumped into why and has some interesting details to share. I also get a chance to share why I suggest that anyone looking for budget-focused shoes might want to think twice about BOA dials.

Then we take some time to answer some listener questions, including a dive into why Mike is adamant that cycling isn’t an expensive sport. That discussion is right around when we also talk about the $6,500 Partington wheels that Pidcock was riding at Worlds. Clearly, the two things are not related. Same story with the 12-speed Dura-Ace Di2 rim brake groupset that apparently still exists for sale.

As you listen, make sure you let us know your thoughts in the comments. We read them all and might discuss your thoughts on the next podcast.

title: Lost generation: the AI threat to Britain’s next great directors
author: Mark Sweney
text:
Commercials once launched careers from Ridley Scott to Guy Ritchie, now automated production is cutting costs – and the chance to learn by doing

W hen Ridley Scott was awarded the UK’s highest accolade for a glittering career directing films from Alien and Blade Runner to Gladiator and The Martian , he reminded those attending the Bafta event eight years ago that making commercials had been his “film school” .

The advertising industry has long been a breeding ground for British film and TV talent who have gone on to make the jump to Hollywood productions , including Guy Ritchie, who started out making music videos and commercials, and Paddington in Peru director Dougal Wilson, whose credits include a number of John Lewis’s famous Christmas ads.

But the panicked race to introduce AI technology across the advertising industry , to cut client costs and avoid being pushed aside by big tech, has raised fears of a lost generation who may be denied the opportunity to develop into great British film and TV directors.

“100%, yes, I have fears,” says Luke Scott, who runs the group that includes Ridley Scott Associates, the media production company that was co-founded by his father in the 1960s.

“I’m grown up enough to recognise that change is inevitable. But what I’ve seen generally in terms of generative AI output is a very mixed bag. You can turn to it and do something and say ‘Look what I made and isn’t it edifying’. But that is very misleading and sort of introducing us to an ersatz creativity.

“The grave danger is the monoculturalisation of everything. The creative business is something you learn by doing. It is in the doing that is most valuable. Flying a drone isn’t like flying, there isn’t that visceral feeling to it, you are not actually flying. What do you do with that lost generation? Maybe in 20 or 30 years the whole notion of the ad industry as we work now will be an [anachronistic] joke.”

Last month, the global advertising group WPP officially opened its flagship production facility in a converted warehouse in east London. It was the first in an international rollout spearheading its £600m WPP Production business, as it aims to bring “world-class creativity and advanced AI capabilities under one roof”.

Cindy Rose, a former Microsoft executive appointed WPP’s CEO to turn around its fortunes, said that AI is ushering in a “golden age of marketing”.

“WPP and the industry as a whole is at a critical inflection point,” she said, against a backdrop of a Ford Capri being shot cruising the streets of an AI-generated Paris. “We have to better leverage the AI advantage we have. We no longer need to spend our clients’ budgets on expensive shoots abroad. We can do it in the studio [and] completely change the economics of our content supply chain. We can deliver content at the speed of culture.”

One industry source said that some ads can be made up to 60% cheaper, which has some clients embracing AI-led ads to “show finance directors they are making savings”, even though the output often looks “cookie cutter” and suffers a creative “erosion from the diminished role of a director”.

On the topic of the automotive sector the source questioned whether, in an increasingly AI-first ad industry, Top Gun would have become the quintessential 1980s blockbuster that it did. The film’s producers, Don Simpson and Jerry Bruckheimer, chose their director, Ridley Scott’s late brother Tony, after seeing a TV ad in which he depicted a Saab car racing a fighter jet in what could pass for a trailer for the cinematic style adopted throughout the film .

However, Richard Glasson, the chief executive of WPP Production, said that new technologies have always been embraced by the industry and the use of AI is no different.

“It is the future of where content is going, an AI production powerhouse for the future,” he said. “The underlying tech we use to create work is changing. It is being introduced in TV and film but not widely adopted in advertising to this point.”

He added that AI is being embraced by clients who need to be able to keep up with creating content across dozens more digital media platforms than ad agencies have ever had to keep pace with.

“All clients need a vastly greater amount of content,” he said. “There has been an explosion in the number of channels that they are talking to their consumers. To win against the algorithms you have to be producing new content, not just repurposing one ad campaign for six months, those days are gone. It is about speed to market, making the previous impossible possible. We can place a brand anywhere in the world in a single afternoon.”

Yet he does not believe that the days of the classic blockbuster ad campaign, and the need for the talent to create award-winning work, are numbered.

“We still make Super Bowl ads that take nine months, football World Cup campaigns and ads with celebrities in exotic locales,” he said. “They still exist and will continue to exist. The elephant in the room is whether AI is coming for jobs, in production we are seeing the opposite. I see AI as an enabler of abundance, and the people working in production as infinitely adaptable and curious about tech and what it will allow us to do.”

title: Arizona Fall League Week 1 Recap
author: Michael Zeno
text:
The Yankees’ contingent is off to a strong start in Arizona.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The first week of the Arizona Fall League is now in the books. Since the league kicked off last Saturday, the Salt River Rafters have played five games and are full of big Yankees contributions through their 4-1 start. All eight of the representatives have gotten in games thus far with mixed levels of results. If you want a quick rundown on who’s in the desert this month, check here .

October 3 (Rafters 9, Desert Dogs 4) : The AFL opener saw five Yankees get into the action. Kyle West looked the best, going 2-for-4 with an RBI and lacing a ball at 109.2 mph. Dax Kilby —the Yankees’ 2025 first-rounder and their star of the show here—ripped a 101.1 mph RBI double and drew a walk, while Core Jackson went 0-for-5 with a walk and two strikeouts. On the pitching side, Anthony Mena allowed a hit in 1.1 scoreless innings, while Mack Estrada got on the mound and walked a pair in 1.1 choppy innings.

October 4 (Rafters 4, Saguaros 6) : The lone defeat of the opening week, only West was in the lineup at first base from the Yankees contingent, going 0-for-4 with a strikeout and a stolen base. He has sneaky speed for a guy who only plays first, having stolen 20 last season. Chris Veach came out of the bullpen in the fourth and got two innings of work in his AFL debut, allowing two runs on three hits and two walks. The highlight of his day was a successful pickoff of Sebastian Walcott to get out of a jam in the fourth.

October 5 (Rafters 10, Javelinas 7) : It got even quieter in the Monday victory over Peoria, where only one Yankee got into the game. Kilby got his second start, leading off and playing shortstop, and was the best player on the field. After striking out in the first, he was perfect the rest of the day. He cracked a 105.1 mph single up the middle in the third, blasted a two-run double off the wall in the fifth, lifted a sacrifice fly in the sixth, and capped his day with a 105.4 mph RBI double to end the day 3-for-4 with four RBIs and two doubles.

Kilby said in an interview that he’s “ working on a swing change ,” and the first looks are clearly promising.

October 6 (Rafters 7, Saguaros 2) : Kilby got into another game on Tuesday, but went 0-for-4 with a strikeout. Jackson smoked a 106.6 mph double in his second start at third base, but the star was West, who had a single and two RBIs. On the pitching side, we got a scoreless inning out of converted catcher Antonio Gomez, who had a walk and a strikeout. He was only up to 98.4 with less ride on his fastball than usual, but that could be for any number of reasons.

October 8 (Rafters 4, Solar Sox 3) : West got another start at first base and went 2-for-4 with an RBI. Both singles were scorched 110 mph, with the latter being a walk-off single. Four different pitchers got into the game, with JT Etheridge tossing 2.2 solid innings to start before giving way to Estrada to finish the inning. Veach walked a pair, but struck out the side in a scoreless inning of his own. Mena finished things off with two innings of his own, allowing a run with two strikeouts. The star of this game? Kilby, who led off the game with a home run to finish off a spectacular first week in the AFL.

Ex-Deutsche Bank trader jailed for rigging rates has conviction overturned
text:
Another former banker sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis has had his conviction overturned following a long-running legal battle.

The Court of Appeal has quashed the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who went to prison in 2018 for "manipulating" the benchmark interest rate, Euribor.

It comes after the same UK court overturned five convictions of ex-Barclays bankers in the rate rigging trials earlier this week.

Bittar, who watched proceedings via video link from Switzerland because he was not granted a visa to attend court, told the BBC: "I have waited a very, very long time for this day."

The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries.

There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts.

The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties.

Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York.

Eighteen of these have now been acquitted.

Only one former trader in the world now remains convicted: former Barclays trader Peter Johnson, who was also one of the original whistleblowers in the interest rate rigging scandal. He pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance at winning at trial. The court confirmed that he too has now applied to appeal against his conviction.

The news has already prompted lawyers and senior politicians to press for the Bank of England and the Treasury to release all their records about their own roles in interest rate 'rigging' during the financial crisis, amid concerns raised of a cover-up of the role of central banks and governments.

Speaking after his conviction was quashed, Bittar said: "Finally the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised.

"I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it."

His wife, Caroline, who lives in the UK, said their family had lost 15 "valuable years", with their children "growing up with this injustice".

She added they were looking forward to "enjoying life with our family and friends without this shadow hanging over us".

On Wednesday, Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham and Philippe Mouryoussef saw their convictions for 'manipulating' the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor quashed after a 10-year struggle for justice.

They launched fresh appeals against their jail sentences following a Supreme Court ruling last year that acquitted Tom Hayes, the first to be jailed for 'rigging' interest rates in 2015, and Carlo Palombo, jailed in 2019.

Tom Hayes, who was initially sentenced to 14 years, reduced on appeal to 11, is now seeking damages from his former employer UBS.

The traders were among 37 City traders and brokers prosecuted for "manipulating" the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor, which track the cost of borrowing cash between the banks and have been used to set the interest rates on millions of mortgages and commercial loans.

The BBC has uncovered evidence of a much larger, state-led 'rigging' of interest rates, under pressure from central banks and governments across the world. Evidence implicating Downing Street and the Bank of England was suppressed throughout the criminal trials.

Former Conservative cabinet minister David Davis told the BBC the innocent traders had been the victims of a series of miscarriages of justice.

He said the people exonerated this week and before were "the victims of a scapegoating exercise which arose as a result of the government's own misbehaviour in lowballing [falsely understating] Libor interest rates themselves, in order to try and rescue the economy after their own self-induced crash in the late 2000s".

In 2015, during the first trial for interest rate 'rigging', of former UBS trader Hayes, Mr Justice Jeremy Cooke decided as a matter of law that any attempt to influence the rates could not be lawful, and that any rate influenced by commercial interest must automatically be false. Judges in the subsequent eight trials followed suit.

However, in July 2025, the Supreme Court decided that all the judges had erred, misdirecting juries that it was wrong as a matter of law. Instead, whether the requests were right or wrong was properly a matter of fact for the jury to decide, not the judge.

All convictions in the United States were overturned in 2022 after an appeal court ruled that there was insufficient evidence that the traders' requests had broken any rules or laws.

title: I've got my own questions on Man City case - Carrick
text:
Manchester United boss Michael Carrick still has his "own questions" over the Manchester City case which he says "affected me personally".

There is a clamour among some for Manchester City to be stripped of their silverware and also be relegated after they were found guilty of multiple Premier League financial rule breaches .

The 45-year-old was on the pitch at Sunderland when he learned City had won their first Premier League title in 2012 thanks to Sergio Aguero's legendary injury time match winner.

He was still part of Jose Mourinho's squad when United finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City side in 2018 and was part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching staff when it happened again in 2020-21.

However, Carrick says getting a title winners' medal years after the event would not make up for missing out at the time.

"In football, the strive to win, the emotion and the feeling about winning, a lot of it is in the moment," he said.

"You can't take that back. It's the moment you strive for. That's essentially what we're all in it for. That's the feeling we all crave.

"The beauty of trying to win trophies is a little bit the journey towards it and then the finale. Does it go for you, does it go against you? Once that's done, there's no getting that back in any direction.

"I'm not getting blasé about it, but regardless of anything, in any sport in history, if later on you get the medal, it doesn't bring the feeling of when you initially win or you don't."

An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

Manchester City have appealed against the decision. City boss Enzo Maresca has said he "trusts" his own club.

If the appeal adheres to strict Premier League guidelines, it should be concluded by Christmas Day, with a verdict to follow in the early part of 2027.

Carrick does not know how the situation will play out. However, as a very close bystander to the event, he feels there has to be a speedy resolution.

"It's thrown up a lot of questions," he said. "Some had answers, some haven't.

"Certainly, I've got my own questions about it. It's affected me personally in different ways over a period of time.

"As it's still not finalised, I think I'll hold that one (whether titles should be reassigned) until later on.

"What I will say is that the sooner it gets sorted, for everyone's benefit, is essential.

"It's unprecedented, a unique situation to be in at this level, with such a huge impact in so many ways. We all need to know what's going to happen."

Meanwhile, United's fans have delivered their own verdict by getting a 'ticker' banner showing the years since Manchester City last won a trophy rehung from the Stretford End.

The banner was initially displayed in 2000, at which point it was 24 years since City's last silverware - the 1976 League Cup.

It was increased by one each year until 2011 when City finally ended their trophy drought by beating Stoke City in the FA Cup final.

However, fans have a new version to display for this weekend's visit of Tottenham to Old Trafford, with the number 50 - signalling the years since their 1976 League Cup triumph, their final silverware before Sheikh Mansour bought the club.

Is £70m Baleba ready for his Man Utd exam?

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta, who spent time as assistant to Guardiola at Manchester City prior to taking charge of the Gunners, echoed Maresca's faith in his former club's leadership team.

"[The] titles absolutely [are] not tainted. I trust the club now, in the future, always. I completely trust the club," Arteta said.

"I will respect the process. It is still an ongoing process that is not resolved because it has been appealed."

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola and Chelsea's Xabi Alonso both stressed the need for patience following City's appeal.

"I think uncertainty is not good for anyone and anyone involved, but the process is ongoing and we have to patient like everyone else and see what happens at the end," Iraola said.

Alonso added: "We need to wait for the final sanctions from the panel. I think they are independent enough to assess all the situations.

"We have to be patient for sure. It is out of our hands, we have to respect the independence of the panel and see what happens."

Everton were deducted 10 points in November 2023 - in a punishment later reduced to six on appeal - and then docked two points in April 2024 in separate cases for breaches of profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

"I wasn't here when it was difficult for Everton, when things were bad," said Toffees boss David Moyes.

"Looking at it now from where I am sitting, it looks terrible that we have been docked points and pay some fines and not that long ago.

"There's other things that have been going on - nearly 10 years ago - that have not been dealt with. I find that really difficult.

"I hope it's not just Everton who are getting picked on here."

Nottingham Forest were another club punished previously for breaching PSR rules, with the City Ground side docked four points in March 2024.

"There is no final verdict right now. That's why I don't see any point to comment on Man City because I can't," said Forest boss Oliver Glasner.

"But let's say in general, if somebody cheats he needs to get punished. If not, then not. And of course, we all hope for the integrity of the game, for the integrity of the Premier League, that the final word is spoken soon.

"But we also know, I think there are thousands of pages to read. I read a book every night, and it takes quite long to read thousands of pages and also then find the final verdict, so it takes a little bit of time. We have to be patient, but yes, it should be soon."

title: 'I would love to see an actual gravel rider winning the jersey' – An established gravel incarnation of Nicole Frain lines up as key hope for home-nation at Nannup Gravel World Championships
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
This is the third UCI Gravel World Championships for Australia's Nicole Frain, and she has been steadily working her way up the ranks, while also plotting out such a solid path in the discipline that it's easy to forget it's only her second season focused completely on gravel.

Back in 2024, when she first lined up at the rainbow jersey race, Frain had been racing on the road for Hess, though the team collapsed late in the season. However, she'd already been racing gravel at times in 2024, with strong results that included a run of seconds in RADL GRVL and the UCI Gravel World Series races of The Gralloch and Houffa and then her first World Championships in Belgium, where Marianne Vos won.

"I think the first year I definitely went in with no expectations, and then I surprised myself getting into a really good position. I had stomach issues, but at least for the race, I did put myself into a really good position if it all came together," said Frain who came over the line in 33rd.

Then in 2025 gravel became the main focus for the former Australian road champion, joining the Ridley team, throwing herself into the UCI Gravel World Series and honing her skills. Impressively she also took the overall victory at the series, which meant a start at the front of the field both packed with and dominated by Dutch riders.

"Last year, I learnt about the dynamic," Frain told in the weeks leading into the race. "In the Netherlands, it was not raced in your national federations. You looked around and you just saw all orange, and you realised all the helmets were also SD Worx, and it was very road rider dominated the last two years."

That second year she came 26th, but it's hard not to think that 2026 promises far more. On Saturday Frain will once again line up in the front section of the field, after taking second overall in the UCI Gravel World Series this year, but many other elements have changed.

For a start the race dynamics are expected to be wholly different his time. For a start, the shift for the first time outside Europe means there is no easy turnaround, and riders from other disciplines can't just drop in for a day, so there is less of a flood of European road professionals than in previous years. On top of that the nature of the course is completely different, heavy on climbing and gravel with more than 84% on the unpaved surfaces. This combination has made it a year where more and more key gravel specialists are turning up, raising the prospect that just maybe this year the road professional podium domination could come to an end.

"I would love to see an actual gravel rider winning the rainbow jersey, just because I think for the sport, seeing that at races will be really valuable," said Frain. "But yeah, of course, the best rider will win."

Just as the race situation has altered, so has Frain herself. Now into her second year as a full time gravel racer, having swapped over to Factor this year, and with an impressive list of wins right from claiming the Oceania Championships at RADL GRVL right at the start of the year to four UCI Gravel World Series race wins and also victory at the Unbound European qualifier of Heathland Gravel.

She has proven that she is a force to be reckoned with on gravel, so hopes are high that Frain could just be a rider who can show off the green and gold colours of the nation's jersey near the front at its home World Championships.

"It's definitely been one of my main targets," said Frain. "I've been putting a lot of the effort around that and prioritising everything into this period, so then it's always a little bit more personal pressure, I guess, because you know you put in a bit more effort here, and so you want to see a good outcome that you feel proud of as well."

There was some interruption to the preparation, with a bout of influenza stopping her in her tracks a couple of months ago, but having worked back from that it's now almost time to see what the results of that work and targeted focus will be.

"Generally it can suit me, if I'm having a good day," said Frain of the 125km course with 3,179m of elevation gain. "It does get more towards that heavy end of climbing for me, but then it's hard for everyone. So yeah, if I'm having a good day, and anybody that is smart about it can come away with a good result there, I think."

Though, no matter what you do in preparation gravel remains unpredictable and sometimes that's a blessing and other times its a curse.

"It's still gravel, and anything can happen. Puncture risk is higher and things like that," said Frain. "So you just try not to put too much emphasis on the race because you just want to be happy with whatever you put in.

"But at the same time, yes, it's super important and it is a good opportunity for me to get a nice result and that would ,of course, be the dream."
