title: Can cyclists actually avoid injuries and illness? Experts examined three years of UAE Team Emirates-XRG data to find out
author: James Witts
text:
Less unusual is an unusual fact: “There are significantly more crashes on the right side than on the left. We can’t explain why. We’re looking into it.” The words of Raaghib Fredericks, UAE Team Emirates-XRG doctor, at this July’s Science & Cycling conference in Barcelona, where the South African presented his provisional findings on the injury and illness rates at the world’s leading cycling team for seasons 2019 to 2021. That crash bias was a footnote to a fascinating hour that revealed why staying injury- and illness-free is the most significant (albeit unsexy) performance boost a team and its riders can enjoy…

“What do we currently know about injuries and illness at WorldTour level?” asks Fredericks. “Very little. There have been nominal studies in this area, including terrific research entitled ‘ by a team led by Dr Thomas Fallon [of Queen’s University Belfast]. We set out to add to Fallon’s work.”

Fredericks’ research covered 30 male cyclists and analysed injury and illness data from the team’s cloud-based medical database, which was updated weekly. He could then compare those rates against training data from TrainingPeaks, the idea being that by pinning down injury and illness rates against factors like training loads, UAE Team Emirates-XRG could integrate protocols and best practice in search of, if not preventing and eliminating, at least ameliorating the impact of injuries and illness, which are significant. “Over the three seasons analysed, we lost 1,920 racing and training days to illness and injury,” he says. “That equates to around two lost days per rider each month.”

That absence varied from one day to months, as in the case of Diego Ulissi , who the team announced in mid-December 2020 would stop training and racing immediately after an irregular heartbeat led to a myocarditis diagnosis . The Italian was given the green light to resume training the following February, before racing again at mid-April’s GP Miguel Indurain. The 37-year-old now races for XDS Astana after making the switch for the 2025 season.

From a team’s perspective, a broken rider is like a broken wheel: useless. His or her impact is felt by the team, with schedules changed and, depending on the rider, chances of victory diminished. The competitive impact is felt commercially, framed against cycling’s fragile business model. Losing your strongest riders equals fewer wins equals less media exposure equals a struggle to attract sponsors… It’s a domino effect of doom.

Injury has a real and quantifiable impact on a rider’s transfer or contract value, too. The European Sport Management Quarterly, Journal of Sports Economics and Applied Economics have all featured research that shows injury can impact market valuation by 10 to 20%, with that rising to over 30% for a serious or recurrent injury. It’s worse news for older riders, as this can approach 50% for those on the wrong side of 28 years old. Naturally, this drop in market value limits an athlete’s salary and earning potential.

Egan Bernal is a clear example. In 2019, the Colombian won the Tour de France at the age of 22. In January 2022, he signed a lucrative five-year extension with Ineos reportedly worth €2.5 million to €3.0 million annually. Later that month, he suffered over 20 broken bones, a punctured lung and chest trauma after hitting a parked bus at 62km/hr . Since then, though he’s shown glimpses of his past form, he’s not been the same rider. His contract with Netcompany Ineos runs out at the end of this year and, at the time of writing, though there are rumours of either another extension or a move to Movistar, his future remains unclear. What is clear is that his likely next deal will see a salary drop to €2 million or less. Still healthy, but a sizeable percentage drop.

Time off the bike has clear consequences, so the aims are prevention (the ideal) and limitation (the reality). In Fredericks’ analysis, those 1,920 lost days were broken down into 140 incidences of injury and 134 incidences of illness.

When it comes to injury, 68% occurred during racing (compared to 32% in training). That’s significant and even more so when you account for annual workload. While training volume nestles between 18,000 and 23,000km, racing is around 8,500km. All in all, a rider is four times more likely to crash during a race than training.

No one was seriously injured, and all riders started the next day. “That was a positive,” says Fredericks. “But I’m just glad I wasn’t the doctor at that race. He had to dress and undress the injured six riders for up to 12 days, adding an extra two-and-a-half hours to his day. Injury has significant implications for the staff as well as the riders.” (The doctor clearly did a fine job. This was the Grand Tour where Pogačar introduced himself to the world, finishing third and winning three stages in the process.)

Jayco AlUla doctor Luca Pollastre agrees that traumatic injuries are the most common. “While the frequency of crashes is relatively stable, the severity of those crashes is rising, which can mean weeks or even months before an athlete can return to competition,” he says. “We feel this is due to the aggressive nature of racing.”

The most common trauma in Fredericks’ analysis was what he euphemistically termed ‘superficial’, like the road rash Pogačar endured at La Vuelta. Then came damage to bones – fractures or breaks – which shines a spotlight on bone health, a hot topic in professional cycling. Fredericks revealed that a significant number of riders [over 50%] had low bone mineral density, and quite a few of them are actually osteoporotic. Treatment includes bone-strengthening medication, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and weight-bearing exercise.

“But that raises an important quandary,” says Fredericks. “We want to protect the riders from the risk of a fracture, but will they be interested in running, which we know helps? And will they be happier for more weights if it adds weight? It’s tricky.”

Damage to muscles, tendons and cartilage followed, while in Fallon’s research, hand and head injuries, particularly fractures and concussions, were common, with head injuries the most prevalent for female riders.

Overuse injuries are far less common, says Fredericks, with the majority related to patellar tendinopathy and Achilles tendinopathy, which are the result of the repetitive load of thousands of pedal strokes outpacing the tendons’ ability to recover and adapt.

Arguably, their rarity is credit to bike-fitters, like Phil Cavell, co-founder of Cyclefit in London, who have worked with many professional riders, including the Lidl-Trek team. Cavell’s also an author, whose most recent book, The Cycling Addiction, has just come out.

“To be fair, bike-fitters are only one reference point WorldTour riders are triangulating off,” says Cavell. “There’s also advice from teams and, surprise, surprise, WorldTour trends. Sometimes riders make decisions not wholly based on bike-fit and physio-led opinion.”

Cavell says there are hotspots when working with WorldTour riders, most notably when myriad factors change, like the bike, shoes, saddle and pedals, which can happen if a team’s sponsors change or a rider moves. “That’s when team camps become dawn to dusk affairs,” he says. “There may be adaptations at the foot, knee, hip, back… These adaptations may express over time, so our job is to predict what’s going to happen and put in place mediations.”

“I remember working with a very good rider, recently retired, who started a particular Grand Tour with a 17cm drop from saddle to bars,” he adds. “It worked okay for eight or nine days until it didn’t. We were brought in to revise his drop with a bit more insight and data – saddle pressure-mapping, motion-capture. He could see his issues reflected in our findings.”

Fredericks’ research also focused on the impact of illness, explicitly seen in February 2020 when the UAE Tour was abandoned with two stages remaining due to an outbreak of Covid-19 at the UAE Team Emirates’ hotel in Abu Dhabi. The Emirati team and three other squads were quarantined for two weeks while health authorities carried out tests. Soon after, the team’s lead sprinter, Fernando Gaviria, confirmed that he had contracted coronavirus.

Of the 134 incidences of illness between 2019 and 2021, Fredericks says that 41% of these occurred during racing, with the remaining 59% either in training or between races. “In that time, we had 11 recorded cases of COVID, resulting in a loss of 137 race days [out of 659 lost to illness as a whole]. That’s significant and came down to the minimum 14-day isolation period, plus a graduated return to racing.”

Obviously other teams suffered. Take Simon Yates at Jayco AlUla, who tested positive after stage seven of the 2020 Giro d’Italia, held in October, and withdrew. The Australian outfit’s staff members also tested positive at both the Giro and late August’s Tour de France. The pandemic’s impact is still felt by Jayco, albeit positively.

“We have systems in place that stem from that experience,” says Pollastre. “These range from the use of face masks to strategic room allocation for athletes and the careful assignment of therapists to individual riders, among many other measures.”

“At the beginning of each season, we strongly recommend influenza vaccination for both staff and athletes,” he continues. “During the season, the team doctors hold a weekly call to review the health status of all riders. Relevant information is then shared with coaches and sports directors to support performance-related decisions. Understanding wearable technology data, training loads and providing continuous education are key components in minimising risk.”

Still, despite best practice, it’s hard to avoid SAD (Seasonal Afflicted Danger). “We always expect more issues at the start of the season due to the weather and changes in environment, moving from Australia to the Middle East and then into the European season,” adds Pollastre. “Towards the end of the year, there can also be a spike in illness due to the cumulative fatigue of the season. Although we haven’t analysed it over seasons, at our team I believe that a loss of approximately 10% of training and racing days per rider per year is a realistic average.”

Pollastre says that upper respiratory infections are the biggest cause of time off the bike, which matches both the data from Fallon and Fredericks’ research: “Of the 134 incidence of illness, 60 were respiratory related, like upper respiratory tract infections.” That’s around 45%. Fallon’s study found that racing Grand Tours is associated with a spike, potentially due to “immunosuppression” through the three-week strain. Load management is one method to reduce the chances of falling ill, but that’s clearly more controllable in training than at a race.

Dermatological issues, like saddle sores, were responsible for 18% of lost days, with gastrointestinal issues close behind – ideally not too close behind – at 17%. Interestingly, in Fallon’s research, female athletes report a higher ‘burden’ of gastrointestinal symptoms than the males, although the reasons are not fully understood. suggested that this disparity could be down to hormonal changes affecting gut motility and sensitivity.

Looking ahead, Fredericks is planning to pore over more recent data in search of solutions. What those solutions are is highlighted by Fallon’s research, which ranges from the use of protective clothing, such as Dyneema-enhanced jerseys to help reduce the number of abrasion-type injuries to neck-strengthening exercises, particularly for female riders, to minimise linear and rotational acceleration of the head during a crash.

“Cycling should also embrace technological advances in the use of head-impact accelerometers that feedback to the race doctor’s car to improve care and assessment,” the paper reads.…

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘We will remain solely focused on preparing for the start of the season’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
The Knicks lost their second consecutive official scrimmage on Thursday…

…only for the organization to announce on Friday morning that nope, they ain’t budging and entering contract-extension negotiations any time soon.

Gotta love how the outside world sees this as the excrement hitting the fan while we are here resting easy still enjoying the championship.

On the plans for extension-eligible Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, and Deuce McBride:

“As an organization, our entire focus is on preparing for the upcoming season and delivering another year for our fans to be proud of. As a result, we will not be negotiating contract extensions until later in the season and will remain solely focused on preparing for the start of the season.”

On the Knicks’ announcement:

On why the Knicks needed additional time away from basketball after winning the championship:

“If you think about it, we played a long time last year, and our summer was short. So the guys needed to get away from the game. They needed to go fill their cup, however that may be.

“And so our demands weren’t the same as other teams. Going around the league and talking to other teams since they’ve come back, some of them have been working since July and August in terms of training camps here and overseas camps and in [Los Angeles] and Miami and voluntary camps and back in the home gym.

“We encouraged our guys to get back at the end of September, but it wasn’t mandatory. We didn’t really push hard for our vets to come back. I told them to fill, whatever they wanted to do, and take some time and when you’re ready to come back, come back.”

On his straightforward approach to free agency:

“It was pretty chill, honestly. I knew I wanted to come back here, so it was easy.”

On not considering offers outside of New York’s

“We really didn’t listen to anything else. I told my agent and everybody that I wanted to come back here, and if the money situation worked out, I wanted to come back. Not do anything else.”

On embracing a different role with the Knicks this season:

“I know it’s not my regular role that I’ve played before I got here. But it’s something I’ve fallen in love with, and I love playing my role and playing for this team and playing for each other. I think that was the biggest thing last year that I’ve learned.”

On prioritizing winning over individual statistics:

“For us, it’s not about numbers. It’s all about winning the game and doing anything to win the game. And I think a lot of us put things behind us to make that common goal happen.

“And that’s from the coaching staff to everybody down the line. I think we all got to understand on what it means to be a part of this team and a part of the Knicks. So I think that’s been set, and that’s why I wanted to come back. I love the standard. I love the culture here.”

On seeing the Knicks’ three championships represented on their jerseys:

“I just liked seeing the number three at the back of the jersey, the championship number three.”

On Bruce Brown’s potential contributions to the Knicks:

“I’ve known Bruce for a while. Everything I’ve seen from afar as a competitive I’ve seen in these couple weeks here. I think the things that he can do for us can be very helpful”

On his impression of the Knicks from afar:

“They’re super tight. Great locker room. Goofy, fun crowd to be with and be around. It shows why they won last year”

On how the NBA’s second apron impacts all kind of players:

“I’m sure there is. The new CBA is good for max guys, new free agents and rookie extension guys. The middle guys, it kind of sucks for us. There’s not a lot of people getting that full mid-level”

On playing at Madison Square Garden as a Knick:

“It’s kind of surreal. Grew up a Knicks fan and the fact that I’m sitting in this locker room. I’ve always wondered what this locker room looks like”

On the Clippers’ curse and asking the franchise to change its name:

“I do think the Clippers are cursed. I told [Steve] Ballmer to change the name when he first got here and everyone kind of laughed at me.

“They definitely need to change the name. This…energy is still on this franchise.”

On attempting to fight D’Angelo Russell after the leaked video scandal:

“I tried to get to the arena, they had security and everything. They stopped me at the door, told me I couldn’t come in, take a couple of days off.”

“I had the whole gang with me. It was about to go crazy.”

On his reaction to D’Lo leaking the video:

“I ain’t never been in a situation like that where my teammate just snitched on me. I was like, ‘they’re gonna call me a punk in the media,’ and I’m mad for real, I gotta do something. I gotta show him. I know he’s young, 19, 18 or whatever, but still you don’t do nothing like that.”

On arranging retaliation against Russell’s brother:

“I still had to get him, so while he was playing, a couple friends of mine had to get his brother in the family lounge and all that. I had to get some type of get-back.”

On why the alleged retaliation never became public:

“It’s the Lakers. There’s a lot of things that go on in LA. LA is no place for the weak.”

On the false report that LeBron James confronted him for arriving late to practice:

“Yeah, it sucks, but what can you do? It’s unfortunate. I don’t know. One, I’m sure we can check. I don’t know where that came from. It never happened. And two, at the end of the day, I don’t know — I think we just got to focus on ourselves. There’s going to be a lot of outside noise to pull us apart from what we’re supposed to be and what we’re supposed to accomplish. So, it’s important that we stay together and we keep our eyes down.”

On feeling unfairly targeted by the report:

“Yeah, I mean, I don’t know. One, the question I had was, ‘Why me?’ Those type of things I can’t understand. One, it’s not true. But then again, it’s like, ‘Why me?’ But then again, I guess I’m Joel Embiid. I’ve been in that situation. I don’t usually talk when it comes to those (rumors). So, it feels like I’m an easy target. But yeah, as long as we know who we are. And we just got to stick together.”

title: New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm
author: Christopher Knaus and Ariel Bogle
text:
Exclusive: Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention centres

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.

Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.

The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.

But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.

The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.

On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.

The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.

“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.

“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”

Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.

A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.

That’s despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.

The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.

“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.

The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.

Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.

The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.

“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.

A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:

“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”

The Australian Border Force was contacted for comment.

title: Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
author: Jason Burke
text:
Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice

If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.

Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International .

In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.

In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.

Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.

Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.

Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.

Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.

In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook .

The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.

In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.

Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December . Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.

Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.

In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran , its highest number of executions in decades.

Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.

“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

title: Lotto-Intermarché youngster announces retirement from racing after just two years in the peloton
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Lotto-Intermarché youngster Robin Orins has announced his retirement from racing after just two seasons in the professional peloton.

The 24-year-old Belgian turned pro with Lotto-Intermarché last season but missed a large chunk of the year after suffering mental health problems, including panic attacks.

He raced from July to October and took on 27 race days between March and June this season. He announced on Instagram on Thursday that he's decided to retire from racing.

"I’m stepping away from professional cycling," he wrote.

"It’s time to turn a page, filled with emotions, memories and lessons, both positive and negative. A page that shaped me into who I’m today, and one that will be talked about for years to come. It ends earlier than expected, but without regrets."

Orins had excelled as an under-23 rider, claiming second place at the 2024 Liège-Bastogne-Liège U23 as well as two third places at Paris-Roubaix Espoirs, and top-five finishes in the under-23 time trial at the 2024 European and World Championships.

However, Orins struggled upon joining the pro ranks, not making his Lotto-Intermarché debut until the Tour de Wallonie last June.

"The lights just went out. I felt mentally and physically empty. Everything made me tired," Orins said last summer. "I became afraid - of everything, but mostly of myself. I didn’t even have the energy to ride my bike anymore. I lost the joy of cycling."

Last season, he raced Wallonie, the Tour of Britain, and Il Lombardia, among other races. This year, he made his season debut at the GP de Denain and rode several WorldTour races, including Itzulia Basque Country, La Flèche Wallonne, and Liège-Bastogne-Liège .

His most recent outing, and it turns out his final race as a professional, came at the Belgian National Championships in June, where he took part in both the time trial and road race.

"After months of rebuilding myself, I got back on my feet. But I realised how much energy it had taken and how difficult it was to find the old Robin again. No matter how badly I wanted it, the downs were too frequent," Orins wrote.

"This year, I wanted to return happy instead of unhappy. I wanted to enjoy the bike, the people around me, the suffering and, above all, feel fulfilled again. But things didn’t turn out as hoped. No matter how hard I worked, my body said 'no'. Now my head and heart are saying 'no' too."

Orins said his retirement is "like a breath of fresh air", adding that he wants to discover life beyond cycling, which he's done since he was six years old. He did, however, say that his retirement from cycling isn't the end of his sporting ambitions.

"Honestly, this feels like a breath of fresh air. There is more to life than cycling, and I want to discover that with my girlfriend, friends, parents and family.

"Cycling will always have a place in my heart. Every scar, trophy, tear and smile has its story. This is not the end of my sporting ambitions. As my friends say: 'A fox never loses its tricks.'

"Thank you to all the people I love. Cheers! Voske OUT."

title: Mercedes critics think I'm Satan - Wolff
text:
Mercedes Formula 1 boss Toto Wolff says critics who accuse the team of bias against George Russell are "brainless".

The British driver's championship hopes were all but extinguished by an engine failure while he was running third at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last Sunday.

Russell enters this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix 86 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli, and will start from the back because of a grid penalty for using too many engine parts.

Wolff described accusations of favouritism towards Antonelli as "completely nonsensical".

He added: "We've had it in the past with Lewis (Hamilton) fans.

"I mean, literally, I don't know what's going on. Do they think I have a button that says, 'George engine failure now', or disadvantaging one driver against the other when we are fighting for a Constructors' Championship, when we have always had the mindset of providing everybody equal material?

"But I guess this is maybe where social media goes today. People hide behind their screens and then they lash out.

"There's a lot of polarisation going on, and sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team or myself. I'm Satan, I've heard."

Wolff emphasised that he had always pursued a policy of equality between drivers since he took over the leadership of Mercedes in 2013.

He underlined his close personal relationship with Russell and Antonelli, who are both long-time proteges of the team and Wolff personally.

"We have had Kimi since he was 11," Wolff said. "He is an integral part of the team.

"It is very nice to see him grow, be in a position now that he is fighting for a championship at such a young age, the talent he has.

"And then on the other side, George, who has been with us since he was 17, someone that I feel a lot of, how can I say, emotions for and compassion. We are very close."

He said he and his wife Susie socialise with Russell and his fiancee Carmen Montero Mundt.

"We are spending time with Carmen and Susie off the track with each other," he said. "If people would see that we're travelling together, we're having coffee in the same coffee shop, we're going to the gym.

"That's why it's pretty annoying to have some lunatics that have no understanding really about how relationships work coming up with these kinds of accusations.

"So, I don't pay any attention to this. Most important is that George knows how the team is and Kimi knows, and we will always try to give them equal opportunity."

He said a "good example" of the equal treatment of both drivers was this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

The team has decided to split the specification of its cars at Marina Bay after an upgrade in Malaysia last weekend failed to provide the expected step forward in performance.

Russell is using the previous spec car and Antonelli the new one.

Wolff said: "We don't know which one is going to be quicker."

He said initial indications were that the "new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive - not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it.

"The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point. That is one free practice session, and it will be needing more time to really come to more conclusive information."

He said the success or otherwise of the upgrade, Mercedes' first significant change to the car's design since June, could have significant ramifications on Mercedes' preparations for 2027.

"We've put a few months of upgrades into the car, clearly pointing in a direction that we think is advantageous," Wolff said, "and maybe we just need to calibrate it a little bit in order to find the right way forward for 2027."

title: Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC
author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
text:
Exclusive: Chancellor urged to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s tax surcharge cuts to claw back billions in lost revenue

Tax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues, according to campaigners, who are calling on the chancellor, John Healey , to increase taxes and force lenders to pay their “fair share” in the budget.

Calculations by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents unions with more than 5.3 million members across England and Wales, shows that the public purse is billions of pounds worse off as a result of tax cuts introduced under the Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt in 2023.

The then government agreed to slash the bank surcharge – an additional levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% that year. The move was meant to offset a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%, after the industry argued higher taxes would put them at a competitive disadvantage compared with other big financial centres such as New York.

However, the cuts came just as lenders started reaping handsome earnings, thanks to rising interest rates . The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have now generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.

The TUC says the 2023 cuts ultimately robbed the UK purse of tax revenues. Its analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the UK public lost out £2.3bn in 2023-24, a further £1.7bn in 2024-25, and £2bn in 2025-26 – totalling £6bn over three years.

With banks pocketing record profits, the TUC said the surcharge should now be increased beyond its pre-2023 level at the 28 October budget. That could raise up to £60bn, which could be used to cover rising household bills as part of prime minister Andy Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living.

“The Tories’ tax break for banks has cost the UK public purse £6bn and counting. It’s time to end it and to make sure banks pay their fair share,” the TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said.

“At a time when families are struggling with soaring energy costs, taxing banks’ booming profits to cut bills is just plain common sense. There is a mountain of evidence to suggest that banks can afford to pay more tax – not least the record £25bn bonus pool they paid out last year.

“This month’s budget is an opportunity to put things right.”

Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises, after narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, warned Burnham and Healey against further levies during a meeting last month, saying it could put investment and jobs at risk.

Earlier this year, Dimon warned that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile to banks.

The TUC has said raising the surcharge to 16% – double the rate prior to Conservative cuts – could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years. Meanwhile, a 35% bank surcharge, which would match the windfall tax rate that Conservatives imposed on energy companies, would deliver £60bn over four years. Even reversing the surcharge cuts and setting it at 8% would raise £9bn over that same period, the union body said.

“Reversing the last government’s tax cuts is the very least this government can do to claw back some of the lost billions it’s handed to banks in recent years,” said a spokesperson for campaign group Positive Money, which has also been pushing for bank tax rises at the budget. “Banks are making record profits without lifting a finger, thanks to the higher rates being paid to them, by both customers and the Bank of England.”

David Postings, the chief executive of banking lobby group UK Finance said that a strong banking sector was essential for a strong UK economy and that profitable lenders would be able to invest in better services for customers, issue more loans, and deliver “returns” – such as shareholder dividends – that supported people’s savings and pensions.

“Banks also make a major contribution to the public finances and already face a materially higher total tax rate in the UK than in other leading financial centres,” he said.

“Further tax increases would weaken the UK’s competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government’s ambition to deliver growth in every postcode.”

title: ‘This is not an anti-tech town’: backlash to datacenter in city once home to IBM
author: Marina Dunbar
text:
Fight in East Fishkill, New York, part of a growing divide over whether AI benefits outweigh enormous downsides

For decades, East Fishkill helped build New York’s tech industry.

The hamlet, located 70 miles north of New York City, was home to a 460-acre campus where IBM researched and manufactured semiconductor chips for nearly 50 years.

So when the news broke in early 2026 that a real estate developer, Treetop Companies, was exploring plans for what could become one of the largest artificial intelligence (AI) datacenters in the country, a roughly 1-gigawatt campus spanning more than 1m sq ft across about 143 acres, it seemed the town would welcome a new phase in its technological evolution.

Instead, a furious backlash erupted before even a single permit application was filed with the municipal government. Residents began attending town board meetings, organizing rallies and advocating for a temporary ban.

Even before any plans for the facility were drawn up, East Fishkill’s existing zoning laws did not allow for the construction of large datacenters. The town issued a three-year moratorium on them anyway, a sign of the extreme ire against datacenters.

The temporary ban, adopted unanimously in late June, forbids the town from considering new datacenters larger than 20 megawatts until July of 2029, while officials study their potential impacts on water resources and local ecosystems. The development company at the center of the controversy has appealed the measure.

“I just think that we’re at this moment where things are happening very quickly, we need to get our ducks in a row and think about the various ways in which datacenters and new energy usage will affect our long-term community cohesiveness, environmental quality, and character,” said East Fishkill resident and professor Tanya Radford.

The fight unfolding in East Fishkill is a single piece of a growing divide . Both rural towns and communities that once eagerly welcomed hi-tech development are increasingly questioning whether AI infrastructure adds enough local benefit to justify its enormous appetite for electricity, water and land.

“This is not an anti-tech town,” said Radford. “I’m an educator. I use technology.”

The saga began after Treetop Development purchased property in East Fishkill, initially pursuing approvals for a warehouse development. Residents later discovered that the company, through local property owner Donovan Drive Holdings, had entered the queue to have a project approved that would use approximately 1,000 megawatts of electrical service, an amount more consistent with a large-scale AI datacenter than a warehouse.

This request for approval was not submitted to the town of East Fishkill. Rather, it was submitted to New York Independent System Operator (NYISO)’s interconnection queue. NYISO is an independent organization responsible for managing New York’s high-voltage power grid, meaning whenever a company wants to build a big new project, it must formally ask NYISO for permission to connect to the grid.

For those that call East Fishkill home, the NYISO filing quickly raised concerns.

The proposed datacenter would consume more electricity than the entire city of Buffalo, which has about 275,000 people. East Fishkill is home to just 30,000.

“Residents have been speaking out against it to stop any application from coming into the town for the datacenter,” said Melissa Hoffmann, an East Fishkill resident and organizer with a local chapter of Food & Water Watch, an environmental advocacy non-profit.

But because no formal application had been filed with East Fishkill, town officials repeatedly stressed that there was nothing before the planning board to review or reject.

“There is no application before the Town. There has never been an application for a datacenter,” the East Fishkill supervisor Nick D’Alessandro wrote on Facebook in June. D’Alessandro later took down the post. His office did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

He stressed that standalone datacenters were “not even listed as a permissible use” under the town’s zoning laws. Nonetheless, in June the board banned their construction for three years “to give our community certainty and allow time for further study and discussion”.

Hoffmann said months of public pressure ultimately convinced the town board to extend what had initially been discussed as a seven-month pause into a three-year moratorium.

East Fishkill has often been described as an “ innovation hub ”, making opposition to the datacenter proposal remarkable precisely because the town has not been hostile towards new technology.

International Business Machines Corporation, better known as IBM, transformed the town during the latter half of the 20th century into one of the nation’s leading semiconductor manufacturing centers, employing thousands of workers and laying the foundation for what is now iPark 84, home to mixed-use commercial and residential facilities.

Former IBM facilities remain a defining part of the local economy, and iPark continues to house technology companies. One tenant is currently seeking to expand an existing datacenter by approximately 150 megawatts, far smaller than the facility proposed by Treetop.

Residents have insisted that their opposition is not meant to hinder forward-looking tech, but is directed at the unprecedented scale of emerging AI infrastructure.

“The pushback is really to the size,” resident Fran Caracappa, a candidate for county legislature, said. “The Treetop center would be 1,000 megawatts. People do not want to pay higher electricity rates because of a larger datacenter coming in and putting pressure on the grid.”

Residents have also questioned whether the supposed economic benefits justify the costs.

Hoffmann worried that the datacenter would “provide very few jobs”. Caracappa similarly expressed doubt that temporary construction jobs would lead to lasting employment for locals.…

title: Netcompany Ineos add climbers Markel Beloki and Harold Tejada as Sam Welsford exits after just one season
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Netcompany Ineos have announced the arrival of two climbing talents, with Markel Beloki and Harold Tejada both joining the team for 2027, signalling a strengthening of the team’s climbing talent in a bid to return to the team's stage race glories of old.

At the same time, the team will lose sprinter Sam Welsford , who is heading for his home squad Jayco-AlUla on a two-year deal.

Rumours of both Beloki’s and Tejada’s arrival have been long-heralded, though the length of their contracts is unknown, with the British team using the phrase "from 2027" in their press releases.

Both will provide much-needed assistance in the mountains as Netcompany Ineos hope to return to the kind of form that saw them win 12 Grand Tours with five riders across 10 seasons, though they have failed to hit the top step in a single three-week race since Egan Bernal’s Giro d’Italia victory in 2021.

Only 21, Beloki is a strong climber with a huge engine, which brought him second place at the 2024 Spanish National Championships at the age of 18. His two professional wins are also indicators of his potential, with his GC success at this year’s Tour de l’Ain coming off the back of a solo move on a mountain stage in the three-day race.

However, Beloki is yet to show his talents in Grand Tours. His results so far are nothing to write home about, as he failed to finish this year’s Vuelta a España, though a steady 35th overall in the Giro is decent for one so young.

“My ambition is to develop as a stage racer and, in time, compete for results in the Grand Tours," Beloki said.

"I know that it takes patience and consistent work, so being able to learn from experienced teammates, contribute to their success and make the most of my own opportunities is something that really motivates me."

At 29, Tejada is already proven, and while he’s not a regular winner, indeed he has just two pro victories; his most recent success came earlier in 2026 when he won a mountainous sixth stage of Paris-Nice.

“Harold is a strong, solid climber with plenty of experience. He’s been consistently up there over the last few years, and he’ll be a great support to our GC riders," said the team’s cirector of racing, Geraint Thomas.

Heading out of Netcompany Ineos’s roster, which currently stands at only 16 confirmed riders for 2027, is Sam Welsford, the Australian sprinter who has spent just one season at the team. 30-year-old Welsford is heading for Jayco-AlUla , where he’s signed for two years.

Clearly talented, his season at Netcompany has not been as rewarding as both he and the team would have hoped, despite starting the season with a stage win at the Tour Down Under . Since then, he’s struggled for results, finishing in the top 10 on only six occasions, arguably not enough for a sprinter.

His departure might also indicate Netcompany’s increased focus on stage racing, where they’ve historically been so successful, and also be a side effect of Dorian Godon’s success in punchy sprints.

As Netcompany Ineos have chased Beloki, Jayco have been after Welsford for some time. "It is really great that we have been able to finalise this deal and have him on our roster for the next two seasons," said the team’s head of performance, Gene Bates.

"Sam is well known to the team staff and riders. We are really looking forward to working with Sam and his abilities on the road. He is really focussing on road racing now and in the sprints. He will add a great deal of motivation to the group, and having him allows us to focus on some big projects for 2027 and 2028."

Welsford has ridden for a number of WorldTour teams since joining DSM in 2022, but sees this move as a homecoming.

"After five years racing at the highest level, it feels like the right time to come home and be part of an Australian team with such a strong history in the sport," he said.

"I’m looking forward to bringing my experience, continuing to develop and, most importantly, racing for something that feels very close to home. I’m really motivated to see what we can achieve together and proud to represent Australia on the world stage."

title: Anthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systems
text:
Anthropic has raised eyebrows by announcing it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards its AI.

The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior.

It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery.

While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools.

The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances.

But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear.

Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare".

But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it " deeply wrong , external " and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals.

"You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn , external .

"This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not."

Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human , reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji.

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

The people who think AI might become conscious

The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm.

It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom , it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections".

Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons.

But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots.

It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools.

Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you.

Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses.

When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was , external "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know".

The Collins Dictionary meanwhile last November highlighted the re-emergence of the term "clanker" for disparagingly referring to AI tools .

Used to describe robots in Star Wars games and movies since the mid 2000s, the term made its shortlist of words reflecting the mood of 2025 after last July saw many take to TikTok to share their frustrations with AI-powered machines.

Some experts have also posited that being rude to AI chatbots could adversely impact human communication, by seeping into how we talk to and treat others.

title: Brutal Video Shows Four Cyclists Riding Over Thomas Silva’s Legs After Crash
author: ahood
text:
Thomas Silva, inset, was not seriously injured in the crash at Gran Piemonte. (Photo: Getty Images/Instagram)

Thomas Silva crashed at the final corner of Gran Piemonte on Thursday and four riders rode over him in the latest harrowing scene from a bruising week of racing in Italy .

Roadside footage captured by a fan shows the XDS-Astana rider screaming in pain as the peloton speeds past and a few even ride over his legs.

Silva was charging toward the line before he overcooked a right-hander and slammed into the fencing.

He slipped onto the asphalt and his legs were splayed into the pathway of the oncoming bunch. At least four riders struck his legs before Silva curled into the fetal position.

It’s a brutal sequence to watch. Fans frantically wave at approaching riders to slow down and steer clear, but Silva was directly in their path and there was nowhere to go for some of the ongoing riders.

Incredibly, Silva managed to stand up, get back on the bike, and finish 90th.

Team officials confirmed to Velo on Friday that the Uruguayan escaped serious injury in what was his final race of 2026.

“We had the mind and situation to end the season differently. We had a very nice season,” Silva wrote on social media. “But no complaints, thanks for the trust team!”

XDS-Astana’s Alberto Bettiol pushed on to take third behind winner Dorian Godon (Netcompany-Ineos) and Anthon Charmig (Uno-X).

Everything was coming together for Silva until the final corner.

“We were in the perfect position. Unfortunately, Thomas crashed on the final corner and wasn’t there in the final sprint,” Bettiol said. “Otherwise, I really believe we could have finished first and second. But in the end, I took third place and I’m happy with the result in the end of the season.”

For Silva, 24, it was a painful way to end a breakout season.

He won a Giro d’Italia stage and wore the maglia rosa , won back-to-back one-day wins in Spain, and a stage plus the overall at the Arctic Race of Norway.

Silva recently extended his contract through 2029, and Thursday was his last scheduled race of 2026.

Silva’s crash was the latest in a disturbing string of viral clips in a week of high-profile incidents and safety miscues across Italy.

At Monday’s Coppa Bernocchi , a DHL delivery van pulled onto the route after the breakaway passed with about 19km remaining.

Nobody crashed in that incident, and organizers later apologized.

A separate high-speed crash near the finish left Andrea Raccagni (Soudal Quick-Step) with a fractured neck vertebra. Cofidis rider Alex Aranburu fractured his collarbone and part of his pelvis.

At Tuesday’s Tre Valli Varesine, Marcel Camprubí and Thomas Gloag were involved in a collision with a police motorcycle traveling against the direction of the race .

Camprubí continued, but Gloag abandoned and needed stitches in his knee. Their Pinarello-Q36.5 captain Tom Pidcock said he was so angry he considered stopping before continuing to finish second.

“We were going 70kph on a descent and went into a round-about. We saw a motorbike coming towards us, and Thomas Gloag and me, we hit the bike,” Camprubí told Eurosport . “We are both really lucky that we were not in the hospital.

“It’s a bit frustrating, because these things happen and happen and happen, and nothing changes,” he said. “We are waiting for the facts. The team is speaking with the organization and the police, and we are still waiting for the responses.

“I think everybody can make mistakes, but when we are talking about life, we should be a bit more cautious.”

All eyes will be on Il Lombardia on Saturday, the season’s final monument and the last major race for some of the biggest stars in the elite men’s peloton.

title: A rare return to unpredictability as no Tadej Pogačar at Il Lombardia opens the door to the same anarchy as Worlds – Analysis
author: James Moultrie
text:
In the 25 Monument Classics since Tadej Pogačar won his first of cycling's oldest, most prestigious and hardest one-day races at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2023, 19 of the victories have been shared only by him and Mathieu van der Poel, with just seven different winners.

The five other champions in that period are far from complete shocks: Remco Evenepoel twice, Wout van Aert, Matej Mohorič, Jasper Philipsen, and Dylan van Baarle.

All more than 230km in length and offering up some of the most attritional routes seen on the cycling calendar, the Monuments have long been where the preeminent riders rise to the top, but even the era immediately preceding the arrival of Pogačar pointed to more of a democracy than the almost total duopoly we've been watching for the past four seasons.

In the 25 Monument Classics before Pogačar sprinted to that maiden title in Liège, there were 22 different winners across Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix, Liège, and Il Lombardia , with only Jakob Fuglsang, Vincenzo Nibali, and Phillipe Gilbert as repeat champions in that time frame, and considerably more riders in play for the wins.

As 2026 nears the final of the five, Il Lombardia, on Saturday, the racing should briefly be returned to the less predictable and – if the World Championships men's road race was anything to go by – almost completely lawless racing largely unseen since the Slovenian has established a vice grip on the majority of major races.

Just as San Remo was for Eddy Merckx, Roubaix was for Roger De Vlaeminck, and Lombardy was for Fausto Coppi, Pogačar has made one of the five his particular playground of choice, and that has been the northern Italian race, matching the latter's record of five victories as he completely destroyed the field 12 months ago to maintain his perfect record.

And anything but the sixth arriving this Autumn, and Italy's greatest rider being overtaken 72 years after he set what seemed like an unbreakable record, would've been one of the shocks of the season, no matter who was on the start list.

But even Pogačar – despite his miraculous ability to avoid major injuries for the large majority of his career – is not invincible, and the most important crash in terms of impact all season , which left him concussed and with a fractured collarbone and vertebrae at the Vuelta a España, has changed the complexion of what likely would've otherwise been another tension-less Il Lombardia.

Throughout his reign of five wins, the Slovenian has only grown more dominant as the years went on, too, winning his first two titles from two-up sprints against Fausto Masnada and Enric Mas – who showed the world exactly how to step into the void left by Pogačar as he soared to the Vuelta a España GC title last month , Spain's first for 12 years.

But the unchanged variable of his perfect record has been UAE controlling the race on the approach to whatever the key climb is on the route, and preventing any of the previous chaos, randomness, and masterclasses at the eleventh hour of the season which long punctuated Lombardias gone by into the 2020s – shown best by the list of former winners – from developing.

In truth, Pogačar is so superior that UAE haven't needed to rely on overly nuanced tactics whether heading to Bergamo or Como, instead just setting a brutal tempo before launching him into the final 30-50km, and to three solo wins at the last three editions – winning by 0:52 in 2023, a massive 3:16 in 2024, and 1:48 last season.

The runner-up in those latter two was Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), who seems the obvious successor on paper. However, as everyone saw at Worlds in Montreal, where that same theory was tested, the Belgian star is significantly less of a guarantee than his contemporary.

What became clear in Canada is that the gap between Pogačar and the rest is much greater than that of the rest to each other, with Evenepoel likely starting on a par with UAE's leaders Isaac del Toro and World Champion Brandon McNulty, Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM), Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5), Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek), and Matteo Jorgenson (Visma-Lease a Bike).

Evenepoel going solo seemed likely before he was brought back down to earth in Canada , and while he can try to just follow the moves and somewhat rely on his sprint, the millimetres and controversial photo finish that saw him snatch the European title from Ciccone's grasp leave cause for nerves to creep in.

Pogačar's brute force approach is what benefitted the Belgian most, particularly last year, with the earlier and earlier opening up of races ruling out anyone from even attempting to beat the UAE rider tactically.

But thinking he can match that as the instigator could prove fatal for Evenepoel and Red Bull's chances, as it's easy to forget what the reigning champion has normalised when it comes to solo attacking, often matching records set by Merckx and Coppi with his daring, but now expected moves.

With that should come what was true of Worlds: a war of attrition being matched by a total tactical battle, where the numbers game may prove as vital as it did for McNulty and the USA en route to rainbows. Evenepoel's greatest asset may end up not being his ability to solo or sprint, but whether Primož Roglič or Giulio Pellizzari can make it into the leading split to add more strings to his attacking bow, and the same can be said of UAE, who are probably still starting with the strongest team.

McNulty and the US showed everyone the blueprint for how to win a Pogačar-less race at Worlds, and it was actually his compatriot Quinn Simmons who came closest to upsetting the usual flow of Lombardy a year ago when he made an all-out assault on the course from the early breakaway.

UAE and Pogačar hoovered him up eventually, of course, and he faded to fourth by the time the race reached the finish, but knowing that the bullet from behind won't be anywhere near as threatening compared to the inevitability of the Slovenian, it could cause the early break to return as a genuine method to victory.

Don't be surprised to see the stars and stripes of Simmons and several others all on the move to try and get ahead of Evenepoel, Del Toro and Seixas, as anticipation becomes genuinely threatening again. However, this would be returning cycling to an even older era if someone were able to pull it off, and the difficulty of the route cannot be sniffed at with 4,845m of elevation gain packed into the 243km.

Mollema in 2019 provides the blueprint

It feels like a lifetime ago that George Bennett was battling away with the Astana duo of Fuglsang and Aleksandr Vlasov until the last 6km of the COVID-19-rescheduled 2020 edition in August of that year, or since Bauke Mollema's well-timed move in the last 20km of the 2019 race saw him emerge victorious ahead of a group of closely matched climbing stars like Roglič, Egan Bernal, and Alejandro Valverde.

What was then an attainable goal for many, Il Lombardia became unwinnable in the years that followed for 99% of the peloton, and the same can largely be said of the other four Monuments. But with the door now open in Pogačar's absence, perhaps the biggest surprise win since Mohorić in San Remo in 2022 is around the corner – and even then San Remo has long stood as the most unpredictable of the five, so that run of predictable winners likely stretches back even further.

Despite their importance in the context of cycling's history and Pogačar's place as an all-time great, the past three editions could have been an email in reality, with everyone, including his rivals, without wanting to admit it, knowing who was going to win barring major incidents.

With the Slovenian returning to action in 2027, it may be the only chance some riders get to win a Monument for the next six years [when his newly-signed contract ends], so they must grasp it with both hands.

Few outcomes would be as compelling as Evenepoel emerging victorious, though, six years on from the horror crash off a bridge which left him seriously injured and leaving the race in an ambulance. But it's hard to see anything but an incredibly complex race play out for the Belgian, so he will have to thrive amid the adversity as he did at the Euros and several races before. If he does succeed, the outpouring of emotion should be cathartic.

Mollema will start Saturday's race as the oldest rider at 39, before his retirement, and it's his method to victory which looks most likely: all the big names together in the last 30km, before someone makes the right opportunistic move, and perhaps that could come from Evenepoel, or Seixas, the youngest man on the start line. This Saturday's race and a return to a more open Il Lombardia won't be one to miss.

title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence
author: Adam Morton in Nadi, Fiji
text:
‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji

Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.

But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.

Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.

Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations.

Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.

But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.

On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu , a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.

In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.

Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.

Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.”

The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating would reach at least 1.8C , well beyond the 1.5C ceiling of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses.

Throughout the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for poor and vulnerable communities who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised.

Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority of Cop31 .”

Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk.

Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.”

“The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.”

Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehicles coming from electricity by 2035. Now it is about 21%.

But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed.

Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global community at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago . But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing to back new coal and gas developments and being largely silent before the pre-Cop on the need to phase out fossil fuels.

Bowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants.

Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states, strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil.…

title: Thieves make off with €5m haul from prestigious Italian winery
author: Angela Giuffrida in Rome
text:
Gang breaks into cellar of Marchesi Antinori in Cortona and loads two trucks with 30,000 bottles before getaway

Thousands of bottles of wine worth €5m (£4.2m) have been stolen from a prestigious winery in Tuscany in what is thought to be the biggest heist of its kind in Italy .

A gang of at least seven masked individuals broke into the cellar of Marchesi Antinori, a family-owned winery dating back to the late 1300s, in Cortona after shutting off the alarms and surveillance cameras before using company forklifts to load two large trucks with 30,000 bottles of wine and making off.

Among the bottles targeted were those most prized by wine collectors and consumers, including Solaia, Guado al Tasso and Tignanello, notable as one of the first red wines in the Tuscany region to be produced without white grapes. All the stolen bottles, ranging in price between €120 and €400 a bottle, are from the firm’s 2023 vintage.

The theft occurred on Saturday as the company, based in the hilltop town of Cortona, prepared for a major shipment to buyers abroad. The robbery was discovered only when staff arrived for work on Monday morning.

“The gang was very prepared,” Renzo Cotarella, chief executive of Marchesi Antinori, told Corriere della Sera . “A theft of this scale and value has never happened before in Italy.”

He said he had “great confidence” that investigators would trace the stolen wine, which included 3,000 bottles, some of them magnum-sized, of Barolo Ginestra.

“Two trucks full of merchandise can’t just disappear into thin air,” he added. “The Tuscan roads are full of cameras. Perhaps with a bit of luck we’ll be able to recover at least some of the bottles.”

There have been several thefts at wineries in Italy in recent months, including one in Alba in the northern Piedmont region in mid-September.

But Cotarella, who suspects the same gang could have been involved, never imagined a theft of such scale would happen to his company. Unfortunately, its insurance policy does not cover the robbery of wine at such huge value.

“We had always considered the possibility of having a few cases of wine being stolen during their transportation, but certainly not that two trucks manage to enter the cellar and make off with such a huge haul,” he told Corriere.

Such large wine robberies were usually meticulously prepared and would probably be carried out by those with an intimate knowledge of wine themselves, Corriere suggested, with the target destination possibly collectors, bars or restaurants. However, a sudden increase in the supply of such wines could raise suspicion.

As the investigators continue their search, Cotarella said the company, which was established in 1385, has warned customers to be wary of any offers of its wine outside official channels.

title: Is Antonelli favoured by Mercedes? Wolff responds to latest claims
'I'm here to just go all-out and race without any regret' – Florian Vermeersch prepared for Gravel Worlds title defence
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Belgian racer Florian Vermeersch is in Australia this weekend, the 27-year-old taking aim to become the first rider to defend the gravel world title since the event was established in 2022.

Now he's in Nannup, Western Australia, for another shot at the UCI Gravel World Championships , where he'll face off against the likes of Keegan Swenson (USA), Mads Würtz Schmidt (Denmark), and Matt Beers (South Africa), among others.

Vermeersch has mostly focussed on the road this season, racing the spring Classics (including podiums at Omloop Het Nieuwsblad and the E3 Saxo Classic plus a top-10 finish at the Tour of Flanders) and the Giro d'Italia. But he's still prepared to defend his title at the Gravel Worlds,

"Unfortunately, I've done only one gravel race. The plan was to do one or two more, but due to my calendar, it was not possible," Vermeersch told this week.

"But I've done a lot of gravel rides at home wearing the jersey, so I've enjoyed that. It was a very nice year, I would say. It's an honour to wear those rainbow colours."

Vermeersch and his UAE Team Emirates-XRG team have planned for him to return to the gravel this week to keep the rainbow stripes in the team along with Brandon McNulty's road world title .

"From December last year, when we were speaking about my calendar with my team, I already got the signal that I could defend my title. They gave me the freedom that if I wanted, I could come here," he said.

"I said immediately that I would like to defend it. So it was a bit of a no-brainer. I didn't really have to fight for it with the team; they allowed me to come, so that's very nice of them and I really appreciate that.

"The last few weeks, to prepare and train for this race, have been very nice. I've made a lot of hours on the bike, and I think I'm in a good place."

The 144km elite men's race route will include 3,713 metres of climbing and much tougher gravel than previous editions in Belgium, Italy, and the Netherlands, with at least 80% gravel on every route, said race director Stephen Gallagher.

"I did the big loop – the 77km loop – yesterday, and it's really tough. I think it's going to be a very demanding race, but I'm in for a challenge, and we'll see," Vermeersch said of the route.

"Some corners were actually pretty sketchy. It's really slippery, and you have to pay attention. But I think now, with the rain coming down, it's going to make it a bit faster and a little bit less slippery in the corners, I think. So for this, the rain is not too bad."

He acknowledged that the route is a major challenge but noted that some pressure is off his shoulders, having already won the world title last time out.

"I think it's going to be on the limit. I'm a big guy, and it's almost 4,000 metres of climbing. But I'm in for a challenge. I really like the course, and we'll see where I end up.

"The good thing is I've already won the jersey once, so this is not an extra stress factor for me. I'm here to just go all-out and race without any regret, I would say. Just leave it all out there."
