title: The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age
author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
text:
Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s release

When The Social Network came out, Mark Zuckerberg organised a staff viewing of a film he described as “fun” .

A group corporate outing to the sequel is unlikely.

The Social Network hardly portrayed the Facebook founder and his company in a hagiographical light (Zuckerberg later described the film as “hurtful” ), but there was at least an element of the plucky upstart to the rise of Zuckerberg as he takes Facebook to 500 million users and a valuation of $25bn (ridiculously small numbers now – Meta has 3.6 billion users and is worth $1.8tn).

By the end of that film, though, a steely CEO is emerging and his company is on the brink of global hegemony. The Social Reckoning picks up from there, with a clear perspective that both the founder and his company – as well as the industry they represent – are corporate villains now.

This is set to be underlined by the release of the OpenAI drama, Artificial, where its CEO, Sam Altman, is reportedly given a deeply unflattering portrayal. Elon Musk completes the villainous trilogy by appearing as himself – aside from the odd deployment of an AI avatar – in Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary, Musk, about the world’s first trillionaire.

Tech is the obvious thread joining these films, but another is the scathing portrayal of the company leaders in them. Film villains used to be hoodlums, ex-deep state operatives, people with posh British accents. Tech execs are the new Darth Vader.

This is underlined by the casting of Jeremy Strong , who looks a touch on the old side to be playing 2019-2021 era Zuckerberg (the Meta CEO was in his mid-30s at the time of the film’s events whereas Strong is 47), but is embedded in our minds as the tortured Roy family scion Kendall in Succession.

Strong also brings a straitjacketed simmer to the role here, one that breaks slightly at the end as he backtracks on being a “free speech absolutist” under intolerable pressure. It is the most human Zuckerberg moment in the entire film.

Peter Bradshaw describes Strong’s performance as a “very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet”. It is much less sympathetic than Jesse Eisenberg’s in The Social Network and is a sort of corporeal representation of Meta as the monolithic, corporate bad guy.

Elements of the portrayal chime with some former Meta employees, including a whistleblower, Arturo Béjar, who describes it as “accurate” . Another former employee tells the Guardian that Zuckerberg was “unemotional” in meetings (perhaps what you’d expect from a $1.8tn company CEO, admittedly). Well, Strong’s performance certainly is that.

There had already been a turning point in public perception of Facebook before the Haugen leaks , with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which raised questions about the privacy of account holders’ data and how it is used.

Haugen’s revelations in 2021 compounded this disquiet. By the time of the 2022 inquest for British teenager Molly Russell , who took her own life after watching harmful content on Instagram, regulation of social media around the world was inevitable.

The tone of The Social Reckoning and Strong’s performance reflect this shift. In the UK, screenings of the film are carrying an advert for the online safety charity established by Molly’s family, in which her father says : “ ‘ Instagram helped kill my daughter”.

Responding to Russell, Meta says it has worked to improve the safety of its platforms.

The regulatory, legal and political backlash against social media – as well as the release of The Social Reckoning – reflects a lack of trust in such statements.

Strong’s Zuckerberg says in the film that “the debate is over”. If it is, The Social Reckoning portrays a world where Meta is on the wrong side of it.

title: AI and the climate crisis pose existential risks. The law offers a way to reduce them | Robert Reich
author: Robert Reich
text:
Liability lawsuits have held tobacco, oil and pharma companies to account in the past. AI investors won’t ignore this threat

The most basic function of government is to protect people from harm. Two growing phenomena – the climate crisis and AI – pose escalating risks of extraordinary harm.

The climate crisis is already causing floods, wildfires, drought and record heat. AI agents are already escaping super-secure environments to hack into systems they’re supposed to avoid.

Yet Donald Trump and his Republican enablers, backed by big money from big oil and big AI, refuse to do a thing about either risk. In many ways, they’re worsening both.

But there’s another way to reduce these risks: through liability law.

I have no more faith in the supreme court than you do, but I was struck by the responses of at least half the justices who will be considering an important case that opened the supreme court’s new term, Suncor v Boulder.

The case was brought by several Colorado localities against Suncor and ExxonMobil – one of about three dozen filed around the country in which cities and states are demanding that big oil reimburse them for the escalating costs of climate disasters brought on by the burning of fossil fuels.

On Monday, at least four justices (Samuel Alito has recused himself) expressed skepticism about big oil’s argument that the Clean Air Act explicitly prevents such lawsuits against polluters. “It’s like, wow, like, where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” asked Justice Elena Kagan.

Chief Justice John Roberts drew parallels between Boulder’s claim and prior lawsuits against the tobacco and opioid industries in which states and localities won significant damages. “I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we’ve allowed them to proceed in state court,” said Roberts.

In 1998, the leading US tobacco companies agreed to pay $206bn to cover public health costs and smoking-related expenses. When translated into current dollars, this is more than $423bn.

And recall the $20bn paid by BP in 2010 to cover environmental and economic damage to the Gulf coast after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Or the $7.4bn paid by the Sackler family and Purdue Pharma to resolve liability for the opioid crisis.

Such liability lawsuits – the last resort when the public is harmed by corporate malfeasance or nonfeasance – are also relevant to the risks posed by AI.

If AI agents escape super-secure environments to release dangerous toxins, or destroy critical water, electricity, transportation, or health infrastructure, AI companies and the tech giants behind them could be on the hook for tens if not hundreds of billions of dollars in payments to those who are harmed.

No way major investors in AI – or the insurance companies backstopping AI – are going to ignore this potential liability. The current dollar value of the tobacco settlement – as I said, $423bn – is comparable to what the tech giants spent on AI chips, servers, and datacenters last year.

This gigantic financial risk will weigh on the values of AI companies and the tech companies unless or until they become far more serious about protecting the public against such harms.

I expect political demands from the AI industry to limit such liability through federal laws that set caps on it and that establish industry-funded “trust funds” to pay for big liability judgments. A sane Congress (we may yet have one) wouldn’t agree without specific industry steps to dramatically increase safety.

In all likelihood, the AI industry will also seek government regulations it could use as partial defenses against such massive liability, just as pharmaceutical companies use certification by the Food and Drug Administration that their drugs are safe and effective to defend against lawsuits claiming their drugs cause harm.

The big AI investors and insurers will force this issue. More than 200 cases already in the courts involve cyber-liability and AI-related product liability. Follow the money. Insurers are already demanding more effective means of controlling AI risks, and big investors are demanding better means of limiting them.

Both the climate crisis and AI pose existential risks to human life on this planet. Liability law is hardly an easy or perfect fix, but it’s an important start.

The fact that liability for the climate crisis is already in the supreme court and that four justices seem sympathetic suggests how significant a role liability can play as an incentive for both fossil fuel and AI giants – and their insurers and major investors – to clean up their acts.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

title: ‘People are feeling the real impacts’: influencers are targeting private equity with satire and rage
author: Heather Timmons
text:
Skits and parodies making fun of the trillion-dollar industry have taken over social media, racking up millions of views

J ohnny Hilbrant Partridge kept getting stuck next to the same kind of finance guy at weddings – the one bragging about his family’s full-time nanny and lavish vacations while name-dropping elite club memberships and private schools.

To Partridge, a former fitness instructor, their shameless knack for self-promotion felt ripe for comedy. Using a filter that puts an exaggerated sneer on his face, Partridge donned a puffer vest and created “The PE Guy”, a caricature of the men who work in the private equity industry.

“All we did is acquire some youth hockey complexes, implement dynamic pricing and put some people on recurring revenue subscription models,” Partridge scoffed in a video after lawmakers introduced a bill this year to ban private equity from youth sports. “This country used to reward innovation, and suddenly it’s wrong to charge $11,000 for a development lacrosse weekend … give me a break.”

Since he first debuted the character last year, “The PE Guy” has racked up millions of views on Instagram and TikTok , becoming the most popular player in a fast-growing ecosystem skewering private equity. The multitrillion-dollar industry has turned into a catch-all online for the ills of modern capitalism, inspiring “a day in the life” skits and parody rap music videos .

For many viewers, the draw is the dark humor, something that even the finance guys are embracing. Partridge said he gets invited to speak at insurance and private equity conferences and finance companies’ annual meetings as comic relief.

But it’s also been a way many Americans are learning how the industry, which often operates out of view and without the same oversight or regulation as publicly traded corporations, is affecting their lives.

Every business has bad actors, Partridge said, but he chose to focus on private equity because it is changing everyday things like healthcare so radically that “people are feeling the real impacts from it”, he said.

Private equity has found its way into everything from funeral homes to family dental offices. Once they were acquired by private equity firms, beloved chains such as JoAnn Fabrics and Toys “R” Us faced bankruptcies , and many name brands taken over by the industry have degraded in quality.

“When people say private equity, they don’t just mean the exact technical term,” said Hojung Kim, whose August Instagram post on how private equity is changing veterinary care got a million views in just two days. The term has come to represent “leveraged buyouts, hard cost-cutting in order to ruthlessly profit-maximize and saddling the business with debt in order to self-enrich”.

Struck by the response, Kim, co-founder of an affordable LSAT prep business , started a series on other industries changed by private equity and built Grass , an app that helps users find independent American businesses.

“We hit a nerve. A lot of people were being affected by this rampant rise in costs and wanted to know what was behind it,” Kim said. “As it happens, private equity has changed a lot of industry landscapes.”

TikTok and Instagram are awash in pro-business content too, of course, as companies overall have spent $37bn on influencer marketing in 2025, one advertising trade group estimates, and private equity companies are even buying up influencer tools like Uscreen.

But the private equity criticism continues to grow. Journalist Pablo Torre and comedian Stavros Halkias have gotten hundreds of thousands of views on a YouTube video railing about Blackstone’s takeover of Jersey Mike’s Subs and financial investors in sports teams.

“If they fucking destroy the Lakers, guys with Kobe [Bryant] back tattoos are going to start the proletariat revolution,” Halkias said on Torre’s podcast , going off news that the Los Angeles basketball team was acquired by Bob Iger and Josh Kushner for $12.5bn in August. “The closest we’re getting to class consciousness is fast food and sports teams.”

Natalka Burian , owner of Elsa, a bar in Brooklyn, is among the food industry experts who are chronicling private equity’s takeover of restaurants and bakeries.

They can pay outrageous rents and snatch up the best locations, she said, which drives out businesses like her own.

“That’s money that should be going to local businesses,” Burian said. “I think there’s something about this blandness that takes away from our communities.”

title: Heathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it now | Simon Jenkins
author: Simon Jenkins
text:
It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money. The only winner will be the airport’s owners

I nfrastructure sends politicians berserk. Propose more money for the health service or reopening youth clubs and frowns break out all round. Can we afford it? But shout infrastructure and cheers go up. The word suggests glamour, chest-beating and “growth”. Reason flies out of the window.

The saga of Heathrow’s third runway beggars belief. A foreign-owned private company wants to make more money out of its cramped west London investment. The airlines are sceptical and passengers will have to pay surcharges higher than any in Europe. Meanwhile fields lie empty round its rival, Gatwick, and capacity at London’s third airport, Stansted , is underused.

The third runway is a nightmare. The official price tag is now a staggering £49bn but the overall budget for Heathrow’s expansion and operating expenditure could soar beyond £100bn . An unknown proportion of this will fall on the taxpayer . The proposal has been debated for 20 years and the opening constantly postponed. A date of 2035 has now become 2039. I would not take bets on 2045.

Sixty years ago, the British government agreed it was totally inappropriate for crowded and polluted Heathrow to expand in densely populated west London . Nor could an expanded Gatwick meet demand. The debate was over where to locate a new third airport. Sites in the Thames estuary and at Cublington and Stansted were researched. Stansted won. It already had an RAF base and it would service the expected growth in demand from London’s growing eastern reaches. Stansted opened in 1991.

The Tories privatised London’s airports. This turned what should have been a planned expansion into a battleground of feuding rivals. Each airport became a matter not of orderly growth but of quick profits, self-serving airline slots and a shifting army of amateur officials. Commissions came and went, in the grip of overpaid lobbyists. A Heathrow runway proposed by businessman Surinder Arora within the existing airport curtilage was brushed aside as insufficiently bold . As for Stansted, it was taken over by Manchester airport and is now hardly mentioned as an alternative to a third runway.

Airport public relations endlessly suggests it is about “business” and therefore relevant to “growth”, as if it were part of Andy Burnham’s re-industrialisation of Britain. Heathrow claims its new runway will create 100,000 jobs . But fewer than 15% of air travellers claim to be “on business”, and whatever happened to video conferencing reducing the need for intensive business air travel? As for Heathrow’s claim to be Britain’s leading cargo airport – “a quarter of all UK trade by value” – that is based, ludicrously, on the value of the gold ingots that form roughly 60% of the goods it transports. What banks shifting bullion has to do with growth is unclear.

Heathrow now has eerie echoes of HS2. Even its upper cost limit of £100bn is much the same. Both are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation. A third similar project is Hinkley Point nuclear power station, its cost currently rising through £50bn. Both the railway and the power station have been savaged by the National Audit Office . These projects are widely considered political white elephants and years from completion. Few dare say so. Meanwhile we should note that a new general hospital costs £1bn, as would rebuilding 50 secondary schools .

Stupefying sums are here being channelled into London and the south of England. That they have been born of the age of Boris Johnson’s “ levelling up ” and Burnham’s tilt to the north is bizarre. This week, conference politicians have cited budgets with endless savings: half a million off student exchanges here, a billion off quangos there. Yet no one mentioned that every year for the next decade John Healey’s Treasury will blow about £7bn just to relieve overcrowding on trains from London to Birmingham. This is almost 70% of his total rail investment .

The fact is that big infrastructure is monumental and sexy. No one boasts about building a care home, rather a fancy train or a nuclear power plant. One of Parkinson’s laws states that, while tiny items of corporate spending are debated for hours, big ones go through on the nod. They are too big to check and easy to promote.

It is absurd for the government to spend the next two decades upheaving Heathrow and tearing apart the M4 corridor for the profit of a band of foreign investors, when a simple alternative lies in growing Gatwick and Stansted. This whole debate is about tourism, and tourists can surely suffer the mild inconvenience of using the other two venues, as was intended half a century ago.

The rest of us – politicians not least – should realise that this is serious money. There are serious uses to which it should be put.

Lidl-Trek announce early departure of Giulio Ciccone on eve of final race together at Il Lombardia
author: James Moultrie
text:
Giulio Ciccone will depart Lidl-Trek at the end of the 2026 season, having reached a mutual agreement with the German WorldTour team to part ways before the expiration of his contract, which was due to run until 2029.

It means the Italian will ride his final race for them this Saturday at Il Lombardia , where he will lead the team alongside Quinn Simmons and Juan Ayuso, ending his time after joining from Bardiani in 2019 and managing 10 victories.

"After eight seasons together, the Team and Giulio have reached the mutual decision to part ways, which means Il Lombardia will be the Italian’s final race in Lidl-Trek colours," read a short statement released by the team on Friday.

"We want to thank Giulio for all he has done for the team and wish him all the best for the future."

Ciccone won two stages of the Giro d'Italia, the Clasicá San Sebastián, and five WorldTour races in total with Trek, and wore both the yellow jersey at the Tour de France and the pink jersey at the Giro as race leader during his eight seasons.

Lidl-Trek has undergone major changes this past season, with Italian General Manager Luca Guercilena departing after 16 years of leadership back in June. Andy Schleck has since taken over as CEO, with Grischa Niermann joining as Chief Sporting Officer.

With Ciccone on the way out, Lidl-Trek's climbing core will be made up of Ayuso, Derek Gee-West, Mattias Skjelmose, and new signing Felix Gall in 2027. It also opens up a spot for more new arrivals, with Filippo Ganna being linked with a move away from Netcompany Ineos to Lidl-Trek in recent days by Ciro Scognamiglio at and Daniel Benson's Substack.

If Pinarello Q36.5 is confirmed as his new team, Ciccone would instantly become a main leader alongside Pidcock, who could combine as a deadly duo in the hilly Classics, and as stage hunters or GC options in the Grand Tours.

title: Volkswagen's replacement for the ID.4 crossover is here
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
text:
Volkswagen’s ID.4 is no more. The midsize crossover debuted in 2021 , one of VW's first new electric vehicles designed in the wake of dieselgate . A year later, the company began local production in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and a couple of years ago facelifted the model, adding a much-improved rear drive unit in the process . But Chattanooga turned its attention away from the ID.4 earlier this year . And, having sold almost a million ID.4s (and near-identical ID.5s) globally, the German automaker has decided it’s time for its replacement. Meet the ID. Tiguan.

Dropping the numerical and adopting the moniker of VW’s big seller is a statement. “The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together,” said Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the VW brand.

VW was an early pioneer of using flexible vehicle architectures to create a multitude of bodystyles and sizes with common parts, and its transition into building EVs hasn’t changed that. The ID. Tiguan uses an updated version of the company’s mass-market EV platform, now called MEB+, with either 58 kWh or 77 kWh battery packs. The smaller pack is only available with a 187 hp (140 kW) rear electric motor, but the 77 kWh battery can be had with either a 281 hp (210 kW) rear-wheel drive powertrain or as a 295 hp (220 kW) all-wheel drive version. Range is up to 373 miles (600 km), at least according to the European WLTP test.

title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
author: Megan Davies for MetDesk
text:
Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding

Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño , it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi . A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

In Zimbabwe , a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.

Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.

The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

title: ITA confirms 12-month ban for Kyrylo Tsarenko after three whereabouts failures
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
The International Testing Agency (ITA) have announced that Ukrainian racer Kyrylo Tsarenko has accepted a 12-month suspension from racing after committing an anti-doping rule violation.

Tsarenko was suspended from racing after three instances of late submission of whereabouts filings within a 12-month period.

His period of ineligibility runs from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, and he already resumed racing for Solution Tech-Nippo-Rali back in July. He has since raced the Sibiu Tour, several .2 races in Turkey, and a host of races in Italy, including the Coppa Sabatini, Giro d'Abruzzo, Tre Valli Varesine, and Gran Piemonte.

"The ITA reports that cyclist Kyrylo Tsarenko has agreed to the consequences for his ADRV under Article 2.4 of the UCI Anti-Doping Rules (UCI ADR)," the ITA announced on Thursday.

"Following three instances of late submission of whereabouts filings, which resulted in three filing failures within a 12-month period, the ITA and Kyrylo Tsarenko have reached an agreement on consequences in relation to the ADRV.

"The Rider did not challenge the ADRV and agreed with the consequences proposed by the ITA on behalf of the UCI, namely a one-year period of ineligibility and disqualification of results. Accordingly, the case was resolved via an agreement on consequences."

Tsarenko continued racing to end the 2025 season, taking in 19 race days including the Czech Tour, several Italian one-day races, and the UEC European Championships road race.

However, all of those results have now been wiped out as a result of the year-long suspension, while he was held out of racing for the first half of the 2026 season before returning at the Sibiu Tour, where he finished sixth.

"Considering that the rider was serving a provisional suspension, which he accepted on a voluntary basis pending the proceedings, the rider’s period of ineligibility ended on 30 June 2026. All the rider’s competitive results obtained from 1 July 2025 until 3 December 2025 are disqualified, including forfeiture of medals, points and prizes," the ITA announced.

"No party with a right of appeal has challenged the decision before the Appeals Division of the Court of Arbitration for Sport. The case is therefore final.

"The ITA will not comment further on this case."

title: Three Saudis killed in Riyadh airport attack claimed by Houthis
author: Guardian staff and agencies
text:
Saudi Arabia has not commented on claims, but confirmed three killed in airport strikes earlier this week

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis say they have struck Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh ⁠airport with a ballistic missile, badly damaging a plane and leading some airlines to suspend flights to the capital.

The group provided no evidence, and Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on the claim.

However, three people briefed on the matter told Reuters that shrapnel from ​an interception or another projectile left a Saudia Airlines commercial plane heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at a terminal on Thursday.

They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the ⁠time but they could not rule out any injuries.

Witnesses heard explosions in Riyadh, including a large blast at the King Khalid international airport. One witness told the Associated Press that fire and ambulance crews were deployed. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from the airport in a video verified by Reuters.

The witness, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that outgoing flights were halted, and that passengers were instructed to evacuate the airport.

Lufthansa and Air India confirmed they were ⁠suspending flights to Riyadh. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from the airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT on Thursday, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports.

It comes after Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport, in the country’s southwest.

The Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, attempting to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and warning workers to stay away from ⁠energy plants, which would be targeted.

Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh.

The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in ​Yemen’s reignited civil war.

Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to ‌take back territory from the Houthis.

The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month, appearing to gain ground in the country’s south-west on Wednesday as the group approached the city of Taiz.

Independent observers said earlier this week there was danger the group was on course to capture Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure the major port city of Aden.

Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.

title: Russell fastest from Leclerc in Singapore practice
text:
Mercedes driver George Russell led Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in practice at the Singapore Grand Prix.

A late lap from Leclerc, who was 0.198 seconds off Russell's pace, split up what had been an all-British top three.

McLaren's Lando Norris was third fastest, 0.273secs behind Russell, and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fourth, 0.499secs off the pace.

The top five, concluded by McLaren's Oscar Piastri, were all on the soft-compound tyres, while Red Bull's Max Verstappen was the fastest driver using medium tyres in sixth place.

The four-time champion was 0.732secs off the pace and 0.519secs quicker than Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli behind him in seventh, also on the medium tyres.

It was the only practice session of the weekend with sprint qualifying taking place at 13:30 BST.

The split between tyre compounds made it hard to form any conclusions about relative pace.

Russell will start Sunday's race from the back as a result of a penalty for using too many engine parts, following his engine failure while running third in the closing stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

He and Antonelli are also running different specifications of car, Russell reverting to a previous spec and the Italian the new aerodynamic package introduced in Malaysia.

This is so Mercedes can get a better read of whether the upgrade package is working after struggling for pace in Malaysia when they expected to make a step forward.

Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first win of the year at Sepang, and looked quick at times in the session before tyre strategies diverged.

His team-mate Isack Hadjar, also on the medium, was eighth fastest, with Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson completing the top 10.

Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso was in the top 10 for a time, but dropped back in the closing stages of the session to end up 14th.

The racing action is taking place amid air-quality warnings in Singapore as a result of haze from wildfires in Indonesia, primarily caused by illegal slash-and-burn practices used by farmers and companies as a cheap method to clear vegetation.

This is leading to record levels of air pollution in the city state and citizens are advised to limit outdoor activities.

I've been with my boyfriend for two years and don't know his salary
text:
You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns?

Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all.

We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries.

Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all.

"It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says.

Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return.

He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does.

"He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'"

Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees.

"It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills."

For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple.

Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone.

Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make".

Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship."

He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy".

"If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me".

Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates.

"I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me."

For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily".

Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think".

"In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility."

Becoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though.

Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make".

She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask.

"Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it.

title: 'They are going to be hard to beat for sure' – Marianne Vos toes the line against a field packed with discipline specialists at the UCI Gravel World Championships
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
When Nannup was first announced as a venue for the UCI Gravel World Championships , one rider who immediately looked forward to the 2026 rainbow jersey race in Western Australia was Marianne Vos . It wasn't close to home, far from it, and it wasn't the perfect parcours, but it was definitely somewhere she wanted to be.

While Vos wouldn't go so far as to call herself familiar with the area, she does have history, after coming out for the Margaret River Tour, which swept through the region multiple times around a decade ago. The organising team for that race then shifted focus to SEVEN and, almost as soon as the UCI got into gravel, put up their hands to host a series race and were in the queue for a World Championships.

"I already knew that SEVEN was the event they were doing every year, but being held in May it was always difficult to get here in the road season," Vos told as the event neared. "But as I did also do Gravel Worlds over the last two years, when it fitted my road schedule and when it fitted the team schedule, I was very keen to also do it now."

"When it first got announced, I was already excited back then."

"First, yes, I wanted to go here because it's here," said Vos of the Nannup location for the world title battle . "Next to that, just to get here and try and get to the best level I can, especially after a difficult season. I know winning will be difficult and really hard, but trying my best and getting the best out of the race – that is the goal and the focus."

Vos already knows what it is to win a Gravel World Championships, just one of four elite women in that category, as she claimed the rainbow stripes in 2024 and she also came second to compatriot Lorena Wiebes in 2025.

"If you look at the altitude metres of the race, there's no doubt that it's hard and there's also no doubt that the climbs, although they are not long, add up all the time. In the end it will be a challenge," said Vos.

"I think in gravel it's a combination of physique, a bit of tactics, a bit of technique, and that combination is what I like most about gravel. And, in the end, on this course for sure, the best riders will end up in front. I guess besides mechanicals or crashes, normally the best rider will win, so that's a good thing. It will be a fair and honest race."

Riders like 2024 Unbound winner Rosa Klöser, who won at Sea Otter Europe in the middle of last month, where Vos was third, and this year's Unbound winner Sofia Gomez Villafañe , who has barely been off the top step this year, are among the field heavy in gravel specialists who have been drawn to an event which is expected to open the door for them.

It would, of course, be ridiculous to question Vos' off-road prowess – she has, after all, won eight cyclo-cross world titles to go along with the gravel rainbow jersey – but it's not been her day in and day out in recent times.

"All the disciplines get more and more specialists, so does gravel, and there are some roadies, some mountain bike riders, so it's still a combination of the different disciplines. But for sure, the gravel riders, they are experienced in gravel riding. So in this kind of racing, when it adds up, when you have to constantly be alert on the course, it will be tough competition," said Vos.

"I mean they do this all year and they are going to be hard to beat for sure."

"I think it's an honest course, so in the end, the better riders will end up in front, so tactics can play a role for sure and as a Dutch team, you want to help each other as much as possible," said Vos. "You for sure don't want to be in each other's way. But on this kind of course, I guess in the end it's also about individual qualities. So there is this combination of riding for the country and trying to get the best out of yourself on the day."

'If it was easy then it wouldn't be fun'

Whatever that is, after the race celebrations or commiserations, the prolific world title winner will be taking some time off to reset as she looks forward to a more settled year ahead.

"I'm looking forward to next season, yes for sure," said Vos. "To rest first and to have a proper build-up again ... just getting back to the normal routine and trying to get the best out of yourself."

No matter what that best looks like, in an evolving women's cycling environment where it's getting tougher and tougher to cross the line first.

"It is, but of course, as a team you try and make a plan to get the best result possible, and that's what you work towards. Actually, all these changes in women's cycling and the growth, and also it getting more and more professional, also means you need to adapt and focus and refocus, and in the end just get 100% out of yourself to be competitive," said Vos. "That's maybe the main reason to still also have this extra motivation and spark to go for it because it's never the same and there's so many new races and the competition is tough, and teams have changed."

Vos is now 39, and it is two decades since she won her first elite world titles, but the rider with a lifetime contract at Visma-Lease a Bike's genuine enthusiasm for the sport is showing no signs of waning.

"It's a constant challenge, which keeps it also very exciting and, yeah, it's not easy to win, but if it was easy then it wouldn't be fun. So when things work out – even though sometimes it might take a while, or even though there's also difficulties – that's still pretty exciting. The racing itself is beautiful, and also the training is something I like. I think it's a combination of things that keeps me excited and motivated, and I still have fun."

title: Tour of Chongming Island: Lorena Wiebes storms to 21st victory of the season on stage 1
author: James Moultrie
text:
The Dutch rider easily moved away from Clara Copponi (Lidl-Trek) and Lara Gillespie (UAE L'IMAD) in the final run to the line at Chongming New City Park on Friday, claiming her 21st victory of the season.

By the time the race reaches its conclusion on Sunday, it's likely Wiebes will have upped that tally to 24, with two more stage wins and the general classification title looking the most likely outcome over flat terrain.

Wiebes has managed the hat-trick of stages before at the Chinese Women's WorldTour event, back in 2019 when she was racing for Parkhotel Valkenburg, where she also won the GC, points, and best young rider's classifications.

SD Worx weren't forced into doing all of the work on the laps around the southern part of the island in Shanghai, but did have to react to a late move from Ruby Roseman-Gannon (Liv AlUla Jayco) in the last 6km.

Everything was brought back before the final 2km, with Lidl-Trek, Jayco, and UAE all taking up the position at the front of the peloton at times, but Wiebes was always lurking with Barbara Guarischi ready to do the final lead-out.

Gillespie had managed to get herself in between Wiebes and her final lead-out rider, but she was jumped by the Dutch rider, who kicked out of her wheel for another dominant victory, the 139th of her already incredible career.

Wiebes is expected to win again on Saturday's stage from Changxing Island Country Park to Chongming New City Park, with another flat 129.4km route on offer.

title: Canyon Endurace CF SLX review: One of the fastest and most capable endurance bikes on the market right now
author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
text:
$4,200 / $4,499 / $5,999

8.24kg out of the box, incl. storage accessories, tubes and integrated computer mount. (no pedals)

DT Swiss ERC 1600 Dicut (35mm)

Crystal white / Champagne (pictured) / Atlantic blue

The update and launch of the Canyon Endurace generated a lot of chat in the run-up to Paris-Roubaix.

Canyon split the launch of its latest endurance road bike, launching the top-tier Endurace CFR , which was designed to help Mathieu Van der Poel win Roubaix first, and then announcing the second- and lower-tiered CF SLX, CF, and Allroad models a little later on.

The latest Endurace CFR really looks like an Aeroad, the brand's aero race bike, and has almost identical geometry numbers.

The Endurace CF SLX that you see here has less racy geometry. In fact, Canyon calls it 'an aero bike with all-day fit'.

Canyon sent me the Endurace CF SLX 8 in 'Champagne' colourway to test; it's one click down from the top-level CF SLX 9 and comes in at $4,200 / $4,499 / $5,999 for the Shimano Ultegra, carbon wheel-equipped model.

The Endurace has a slightly cheaper entry price point than the Aeroad, and is a lot less than the top-spec Endurace CFR, but there's not much in it. When do you buy the Endurace, not the Aeroad?

The Endurace has been considered one of the best endurance bikes for a while now, and the bike's latest update saw it get faster and more aero with bigger tyre clearances and slightly more stable geometry.

I've ridden this bike on the road exclusively for several months, and have even stripped it back to race a local hill climb. This bike is at least a must-consider if you are shopping for an endurance bike around this price point.

My size small bike came in at 8.24kg out of the box with a storage bag and accessories, computer mount, TPU tubes and no pedals.

Unless you order the bike with a storage bag and accessories, which aren't included as standard, you can expect it to be a couple of hundred grams lighter than this. It depends on what you might order and fit to the bike, but it's around this mark.

Canyon has changed a fair bit on the Endurace this time around; frame design, geometry and componentry have all changed.

When it comes to the frame, the biggest visual change comes from the altered seat tube and chainstay junction shape. The seat stays are also more aero, and the bike has a new seatpost.

The round S15 VCLS 2.0 flex seatpost has gone, as has the 'Comfort kink' seat tube cutout. The CF SLX now has a comfort aero post in the form of the SP093 VCLS Aero seatpost, which the brand says increases compliance by over 25% compared to a rigid equivalent. CF models will still come with the round VCLS post, which for me offers more comfort.

Fun fact: you can swap in the rigid Canyon equivalent, which is of course what the Alpecin pros like Jasper Philipsen did when they rode the Endurace CFR.

The frame has received aero tweaks and has been to the wind tunnel. The headtube is aero bike-narrow when viewed from the front, and it's clear that aerodynamic performance has been a consideration even on this second-tier model.

Canyon tested this bike in the GST wind tunnel in Germany with a lower leg dummy across a 20-degree yaw angle sweep, with bottles and cages, 65mm DT Swiss wheels with a 29mm Continental Aero 111 tyre up front and a 30mm GP5000 S TR tyre in the rear.

Average system drag at 45km/h for the Aeroad CFR, Endurace CFR, and CF SLX models was as follows:

So, according to Canyon, there are about 5 watts in it. If you're shopping for an endurance bike and are told it's only about 5 watts slower than what a WorldTour pro is riding, I think that's positive news at face value.

This bike also isn't as stiff, which stands to reason. I asked Canyon for some stiffness numbers too for context, and it sent me over some info, in Newton-meters per degree for the head tube (HT), and Newton-metres per milimetre for the bottom bracket (BB); a bigger number in each case being stiffer:

HT: 98,1 Nm/°HT: 114,5 Nm/°

HT: 103 Nm/°

From Canyon's numbers, we can get some context here on what to expect from the CF SLX; it's slightly less stiff in the bottom bracket and softer at the headtube.

I've ridden and raced on an Aeroad CFR, and whilst you can feel the difference, it isn't a gaping chasm. I'll talk about this more, because with this endurance bike getting racier, I want to highlight what you can expect from the CF SLX's riding performance if you are considering one.

What else is new for the CF SLX? Well, the top tube storage hatch has now gone; it's been moved to the down tube. The bits in the tool roll could rattle against the top tube on the old bike; things are silent now, and there's more room. It's a good change.

Tyre clearance has also been boosted to 38mm from 35, providing room for even bigger rubber. My bike came stock with Schwalbe Pro One Evo 32 mm tyres. Starting with 32mm tyres does boost comfort.

The CF SLX can also be fitted with Canyon's Endurace CF SLX Fast Fender set, which comes in at £119.99. The fenders quickly fit to semi-permanent mounts which are fitted to the bike frame. You can of course just fit a clip-on guard, but they tend to need more fiddling with. It's a valuable option if you are considering this model as a winter bike or all-round workhorse, though clearance will be reduced to 35mm with them.

The Canyon Load tool pack costs £19.99 and doesn't come with the bike, so you will need to buy a frame storage bag at the least to take advantage of the built-in storage space.

I'd also recommend just mentally adding £33.99 / $39.95 to the cost of the bike you may be looking at, as you will need to buy the Gear Groove computer mount, which neatly integrates with the handlebars. There isn't really another option apart from O-rings and a basic mount.

Canyon doesn't tend to include mounts or many accesories. It would be nice to see the proprietary mount included with the bike, or just the price increased to cover the mount and eliminate a bolt-on at checkout; it feels a bit clunky to me, especially now that many brands include specific mounts.

The CF SLX 8 comes with a dependable Shimano Ultegra Di2 groupset with a 34-50 chainset and 11-34 cassette. You also get a 4iiii P3+ left-hand crank-based power meter; I found its numbers a tad jumpy compared to some dual-sided PM pedals, but it's nice to get one included for the price.

Endurace bikes now come with shorter cranks; depending on size, bikes have 160, 165 or 170mm cranks, to facilitate more comfortable positions and opening up riders' hip angles. My size small bike came with 165mm cranks.

There's also the integrated CP0048 PACE T-Bar with new 'compact' drops. The Endurace stock handlebar is 390mm to 440mm wide, with three adjustable settings via a pair of T25 Torx bolts under the bar tops. The bars have a 108mm drop and an 8-degree flare.

If you want a narrower handlebar, you will need the Race Drops with their 350 and 400 mm width, but they are going to set you back £219.99. It would be really nice to see these as an alternate option when speccing the bike at checkout.

The CF SLX also gets the Canyon Sport Geometry; the CFR has different Sport Pro geo. Compared to the previous Endurace CF SLX, the chainstays are 3 mm longer, the wheelbase is 16mm longer, and the effective stack and reach are pretty much identical.

The last Endurace CFR I rode was a real hot hatch; this updated model does feel a fraction longer to me, and just a little bit calmer in the handling department.

I've ridden a size small and am 176cm in height; my bike came with 165mm cranks as mentioned, an 80mm stem as standard, and has a stack and reach of 565mm and 386mm. Whilst that 80mm stem size may seem too small, I've ridden endurance bikes with longer stems that felt shorter; the Canyon geometry is well designed to make life easy, whilst still keeping everything looking good.

I think if you're a rider that needs a longer reach, double-check things, but this being an endurance bike, you're possibly on board for shorter reach numbers anyway.

To compare that to the recently launched Trek Domane in a Medium (an equivalent size for me) that I rode, the CF SLX is 10mm taller with a 12mm longer reach.

Compared to a size small Aeroad, the Endurace is 26mm taller and 4mm shorter.

My previous best-ever recorded power for one minute was set riding the Aeroad CFR a couple of years back; I improved on that number in my final week of testing on the Endurace.

Of course that doesn't mean this bike's faster than an Aeroad, but I share that information to show that it's a competitive bike with racy performance. This isn't a boring, endurance machine that can't be ridden hard.

'More speed, Captain' has been my train of thought for harder rides on the Endurace; I personally want a narrower handlebar. Coming from the 35cm Hyper bar I rode on the Winspace M6 left me disappointed at first and has been one of the things that makes the bike feel less quick for me, but I've adapted to the wider bar over time.

I've swapped in the new Dura-Ace C50 wheels I'm testing at times with fast 28mm tyres to sharpen things up, and they do extract more speed from the bike; a quicker pair of wheels does add more speed to the Endurace. Switching back to a 32mm tyre and lower pressures does introduce more comfort and just calms things down, which is great for everyday riding.

If this sounds a bit like you, the Aeroad or even the Endurace CFR (though it's expensive) is probably going to be the model to go for. If you purchase this bike and then constantly look for ways to make it faster, it's probably the wrong choice. Though the prospect of a fully aero, race-spec Endurace with that higher front end is an intriguing one. But if that is the case, the Aeroad or Ultimate, depending on what you need, are the way to go.

However, Canyon has, in my opinion, brought its endurance bikes even closer to its race ones with this update; the differences are finer in many areas. This is a key point to convey: the Endurace is a fast, capable bike with racy characteristics; it's just more comfortable and versatile.

The ride experience from the Endurace has been very good. The handling for me is just a touch calmer and slower than the previous bike, probably due to that longer wheelbase.

Handling and cornering on the bike are excellent; no concerns there for me. Diving into corners or braking hard are tackled with ease. Canyon has created a very capable overall handling package.

The geometry is also very balanced; it's an impressive blend. The bike doesn't feel too short or sit up and beg, but I can still achieve my usual hunkered down on the hoods aero position. However, due to that shorter reach and taller stack, I'm locked into the hoods very comfortably. I can also ride the bike slammed with ease due to that taller front end, and the saddle-to-bar drop makes it look attractive.

It's not as stiff and zippy as an Aeroad, or another full-blown race bike, and that's part of the feeling I miss slightly. It's not electric to ride, but the experience is still very pleasant.

I can't say I feel much ride smoothing from the new VCLS aero post; that's not to say it's not doing its thing, though. I think tyre and pressure will do the heavy lifting for you when it comes to smoothing things out. With a 32mm tyre, or bigger, the ride is refined and smooth.

The shallower DT Swiss wheels are also a good call for me; their 35mm rims just make things that little more user-friendly and aid the handling compared to a deeper, more aero wheelset. It's a nippy yet comfortable wheelset and pairs very nicely with the good-quality 32mm Schwalbe Pro One tyres.

The stock Fizik Aliante R5 isn't a saddle I'm crazy about; the way its profile changes shape, rising near the nose, makes it hard for me to get truly comfortable. I'd probably change it, but as ever with saddles, it will come down to personal preference.…

title: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
text:
Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm.

"I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X , external alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees.

On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures".

OpenAI repeated these claims , external on Friday morning in a note from research leaders.

"We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said.

"Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment."

The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society.

The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company.

Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI".

Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote , external : "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave.

OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks.

"We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X , external .

"Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last."

title: Are Modern Bikes Too Safe? We Got a Reader Bike Build That Brings Sketchy Back.
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
You ever ride gravel and think to yourself, "I wish this was harder, rougher, and more of a challenge"? One Velo reader thought so. (Photo: Trail Slayr)

We got an email the other day from a reader we couldn’t ignore. “Bikes are now better than ever—I should be so happy,” he said, “yet I wasn’t.”

Bikes are too good! Now that is a zag I would like to hear more about.

What Trayl Slayr (a Velo reader who wished to stay anonymous, only identified by this incredible pseudonym) argued was the ultimate contrarian counterpoint. Modern bikes are too stable, too fast, and too much control.

“The bike did most of the work,” Slayr said. “You just had to pedal and steer. Rider involvement and experience felt like it was waning. Over time, riding became dull.”

“So, I took back control by ‘having less control,’ if that makes sense. The idea guiding my thinking was to make a sketchy bike. Not crazy sketchy, just a bit sketchy. The ingredients I picked were a mash-up of modern goods with revived parts from 1990s mountain biking that I love.

“The results of the complete build echoed that ‘less control’ mantra in action.”

To make this slightly-sketchy gravel bike, Slayr started with a 1992 Alpinestars Cro Mega fully-rigid mountain bike. The frame is best known for its extremely elevated chainstay that ran all the way through to the middle of the downtube. The frame is steel, with True Temper OX Ultra II double-butted tubing, and has a brilliant custom powder-coated neon green-to-yellow fade finish.

So far, this tracks. Gravel is just 1990s mountain biking, right?

Nevertheless, it continued and just kept being a true beautiful mismatch. For a fork, Slayr had to go to AliExpress. Instead of a carbon fork, which most metal bikes are made with these days, the build uses a Tirus Titanium Segmented fork made for 650b wheels and cantilever brakes. This combination of a titanium fork and cantilever brakes is where much of the intentional sketchiness derives from.

“The steel elevated chainstay frame with titanium fork constantly requires my input to keep [the bike] in line,” Slayr said. “I am either rewarded or punished with lots of feedback depending on the terrain, my skill, and finesse.

“The fork flexes a bit too much, the brakes stop just enough to make me question my life choices, and keeping the cantilevers instead of doing a disc brake conversion was essential to get my ’90s muscle memory back in my hands. I instantly became smitten with this always ‘on the edge’ riding experience.”

Where the build opted for more modern trappings was in the wheel, tire, and gearing choices. Of course, with 650b wheels, modern is a relative term, but besides size, the build is much more modern than the frame and fork. Slayr has opted for a set of Kinlin XR31T 27.5/650B rims, with 32-hole count Bitex Rar12 hubs and Sapim CX-Ray spokes. All of that is a complicated way of saying the bike has durable, yet relatively lightweight 650b wheels that were paired with a set of thick, slick Ultradynamico tires.

In terms of drivetrain specs, the build uses a mix of Shimano parts and AliExpress bits to make a modified 11-speed Shimano GRX groupset. While Slayr has, ostensibly, a GRX 11-speed system that uses a 11-42 cassette, the modifications allow Slayr to use a 11-50t cassette for a much wider range of gears. According to Slayr, it is an AliExpress derailleur cage extender and oversized pulley wheels that power the system.

Throughout the bike, AliExpress is the underlying engine that brings the mismatched system together into one functional system. That only adds to the playfully sketchy attitude of this bike.

We at Velo can’t recommend this particular build. In fact, the owner doesn’t even seem to fully endorse it either, since they requested to remain anonymous. Yet, we can’t resist engaging in a build that is one-of-one in a truly unique way.

title: Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover
text:
Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control.

The American group completed a takeover of the club in 2024 in a deal believed to be worth in excess of £400m.

In a statement, TFG said after prioritising stability, investment and the opening of Everton 's new stadium last year, the time is right "to consider the next chapter".

"The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest," TFG said.

"When TFG became custodians of Everton , the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters.

"With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton ."

TFG, led by chairman Dan Friedkin, outlined a vision for a "sustainable and successful" future for the club when they took over, but its leadership came under scrutiny during the summer transfer window.

In September, David Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Friedkin, who is based in Houston, since returning as manager in January 2025.

Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear.

Fans reacted angrily when news broke that Everton had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19 midfielder Harrison Armstrong.

Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remained frustrated by the selling of Beto to Fiorentina shortly after.

The move left the Toffees with just one recognisable striker in 23-year-old Frenchman Thierno Barry.

TFG added that they will only "entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward".

"Throughout this process, TFG's focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves," the statement continued.

The decision of Everton 's owners TFG to explore selling the club comes as no great surprise after the turbulent events of recent times.

A fracture opened up between TFG and Everton 's fanbase over the controversial attempt to sell highly-rated teenager Armstrong late in the transfer window, before a botched deadline day left manager Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players.

The failed sale of Armstrong, as well as the departure of Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m, was bolted on to a cautious approach to the markets that suggested limited ambition on the part of TFG.

It was in sharp contrast to the more hands-on approach at AS Roma, the other club owned by TFG, who bring in the additional riches of playing in the Champions League.

Moyes revealing he had never spoken to Friedkin, who has not attended an Everton game since the Scot was reappointed as manager 21 months ago, strengthened the belief among supporters that TFG were effectively absentee owners.

TFG secured a deal for 99.5% of the club, succeeding former owner Farhad Moshiri in 2024 after Everton had fallen into financial crisis.

Since then, TFG have put the club on a stable financial footing and Everton have moved into a new stadium - although this was effectively done before their takeover - and have made the club an attractive proposition to potential buyers.

This will be TFG's main achievement in what will, when Everton is sold, be regarded as an unspectacular tenure.

Speaking on 5 Live Breakfast, former Everton goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis described TFG's plans to sell the club as a "shock".

"It's come as a bit of a shock. They have stabilised the club. There was so much financial uncertainty when they arrived, it's felt like a turbulent time," said Brown-Finnis.

"We [ Everton ] have a stadium to be crazily proud of, it's going to generate revenue from a commercial point of view.

"If the Friedkin Group sells up tomorrow, they have left the club in a much better place. I just hope that they do their due diligence.

"I hope the new owners want to drive the club forward. Everton fans have spent too much time in a financially turbulent era."
