Will Carlos Baleba fix Manchester United? Three big questions ahead of potential debut
author: Graham Ruthven
text:
As the Premier League returns, we dive into the signing who could boost United’s midfield – or confuse things further

C arlos Baleba cost Manchester United $88.7m (£65m) plus $6.8m (£5m) in add-ons when they signed him from Brighton in August. He may be worth even more now despite the fact that the Cameroonian has yet to debut for his new club. Many United fans are counting on Baleba to be a one-man solution to their early-season problems. No pressure.

An ankle injury kept Baleba on the sidelines as Michael Carrick’s side struggled against Everton, Manchester City and Fulham. The 22-year-old joined United just a few days after the opening-weekend defeat to Hull City, so he’d already had a preview of his new team’s troubles to come. The scale of Baleba’s task has grown since then.

United will return to action against Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday and Baleba could feature. What sort of impact can fans expect? Will everything click into place with him finally in the lineup? Or could Baleba’s introduction confuse things further?

United spent the best part of $200m (£150m) revamping their midfield in the summer transfer window. Andrey Santos joined from Chelsea before Youri Tielemans left Aston Villa to make the move north. Baleba’s capture from Brighton represented the final component of a long-overdue rebuild.

Carrick has used Kobbie Mainoo and Tielemans as a double pivot in United’s last four Premier League outings with mixed results. While Mainoo has impressed, proving to Thomas Tuchel why he might have been wrong to deny him an opportunity at the World Cup for England, Tielemans’s performances have been trickier to analyze.

Statistically, the Belgian’s numbers are strong. Only Noussair Mazraoui and Mainoo are averaging more accurate passes per 90 minutes for United this season than Tielemans, who is also covering the most distance per 90 minutes of any United player. And yet the Old Trafford outfit have been far too open in the center of the pitch.

Whether that’s due to Bruno Fernandes’s positioning and the freedom he is given as a No 10, Tielemans’s weakness in defensive transition or something else, Carrick has yet to find the right balance. This is reflected in the sheer chaos of United’s first five league games: they have won just one and conceded eight.

Baleba has presumably been signed by United to give their midfield some legs. He is known for his defensive ability and athleticism as well as his press resistance in possession. “You need the courage to come out with the ball in difficult and risky areas,” Baleba said in a Sky Sports interview.

This instinct should encourage United supporters. The club has lacked a true two-way midfielder for years, stretching all the way back to the latter stage of the Alex Ferguson era. Paul Pogba was signed to be that player, but was largely misunderstood by a string of different managers who failed to recognise his attacking instincts.

It’s not clear how Carrick will fit Baleba into his new-look midfield considering Mainoo is in the best form of his career and Santos and Tielemans surely joined United on the promise they would be key figures. Dropping Tielemans in particular could further weaken United’s ability on the ball.

Last season, Baleba ranked seventh among his Brighton teammates for accurate passes per 90 minutes. He ranked 16th for big chances created. Some of this was linked to Baleba’s general struggle for form and fitness, but United haven’t exactly signed a natural creator.

Baleba was included in a matchday squad for the first time away to Fulham on 20 September before the international break and played his first minutes in a behind-closed-doors friendly match last week. He could feature against Spurs this weekend, most likely from the bench given his lack of match sharpness.

Spurs have suffered their own midfield issues this season. Roberto De Zerbi is grappling with many of the same problems Carrick is experiencing and so there could be scope for United to control the center of the pitch, especially with Saturday’s match being at Old Trafford.

On the flip side, if Carrick gets the balance of his midfield wrong or introduces Baleba to the lineup before he’s ready it could prove costly. The United manager is under pressure to prove he can point his team in the right direction again. Another underwhelming result could have Carrick fighting for his job.

If United fans expect Baleba to single-handedly fix their team, they could be disappointed by what the Cameroonian is able to offer. There’s only so much one player can do when Carrick is fighting against years of poor recruitment and boardroom mismanagement. At long last, though, United may finally get to see exactly what they paid all that money for.

title: Is £70m Baleba ready for his Man Utd exam?
text:
Carlos Baleba has come a long way since the day he had to pull out of a Cameroon Cup last-16 match due to a school exam.

Now Baleba's exams tend to be restricted to the football field - and a significant one is looming at Old Trafford this weekend.

It is unfair on the 22-year-old to be viewed as the potential saviour of Manchester United's season.

However, at £70m, Baleba was by far the most expensive of United's three major summer signings.

He is also the player earmarked for the holding midfield role Michael Carrick has had trouble filling effectively following Casemiro's exit in May.

United knew Baleba had an ankle injury when they bought him from Brighton on 25 August and they may have to wait until after the international break for the Cameroon midfielder to make his debut.

They were not expecting that they would be 12th in the Premier League, with just one win and five points from their opening five games. In addition, Brighton came from 2-0 down at Old Trafford to deservedly knock them out of the EFL Cup.

So there is no disguising that the pressure is on for Baleba and his new club ahead of the visit of rock-bottom Tottenham before three away trips in a row. Champions League encounters at Atletico Madrid and Como fall either side of a journey across the Pennines to face Leeds.

"Very quick," is the assessment from one United insider of their first impressions of Baleba. "He covers the ground really well."

A handful of training sessions before Baleba was named on the bench for the 1-1 draw at Fulham on 20 September, and a closed doors game against Swiss League outfit Lausanne-Sports on 2 October, when United's international contingent were absent, is a small sample size to form an opinion on.

However, Baleba's speed is something that should bring positive benefits to United's midfield.

Andrey Santos has it; less so Kobbie Mainoo and Youri Tielemans, who have been paired together by Carrick in the last four league games due to their superior technical abilities.

United have been too easy to play through and danger has not been spotted quickly enough.

Carrick's side is one of only four in the top flight yet to keep a clean sheet. They have conceded twice in four out of their seven games in all competitions. Until an answer is found, an upturn in form is difficult to envisage.

Clearly, Baleba must do a bit more than run fast, and his input must be felt in the dressing room as well as on the pitch.

Sources say an understandable initial shyness and nervousness seems to be being overcome. Baleba is not the most confident English speaker, but he has improved significantly since he moved to Brighton from Lille for £23.2m in 2023.

He has struck up a friendship with Amad Diallo. It is coincidence two young players from Africa should be going through their recovery work at the same time, but also helpful that a shared background creates a natural bond that has been built on over the last few weeks.

Amad was even laughing on the video he uploaded onto social media of Baleba poking fun at him after Cameroon beat his Ivory Coast in a friendly on 3 October.

A former team-mate of new France international Leny Yoro at Lille and Bryan Mbeumo at international level, Baleba already has other unexpected relationships at United's Carrington training ground judging by his joking with Patrick Dorgu after the final game of last season at the Amex Stadium.

The key for United is that Baleba produces the performances that lit up his 2024-25 campaign and earned suggestions of a potential move to Real Madrid, rather than those last term which were often below-par.

Suggestions Baleba had his head turned by late interest from United in the summer of 2025 have been dismissed by Brighton sources, although an alternative reason for the dip in form has not been offered.

As it turned out, the background work done by the data and recruitment teams at Carrington 12 months ago was not wasted. After missing out on Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, and with other options deemed unsuitable, United moved for Baleba just before the shock opening-day defeat at Hull, completing the deal just afterwards.

Given they were being quoted significantly more than £100m for the midfielder in August 2025, they regard £70m as good business.

However, Baleba is yet to step on the pitch and as Fernandes has shown in his disappointing early performances for Tottenham, any early assessment of what constitutes a good deal should at least wait for that.

It will be fascinating to see how Baleba and Fernandes match up to each other if they start at Old Trafford, when defeat for either side has the potential to turn early season disappointment into a near crisis.

Baleba's natural jocular personality should help his preparation. He will hope to get the chance to show off his back flip goal celebration – even if an ability to find the net is not why United bought him.

More importantly though, he has a powerful determination to succeed, drilled into him by his dad. He pushed him through punishing training sessions when he was younger, which Baleba has said was integral to him becoming a professional.

In a sense, success has already been achieved given he has fulfilled a promise he made to his mum to build her a house in Douala. Tragically for Baleba, his mother died a few months before he left Lille and never saw it.

He is still pushing, still motivated to do well for her, as he recounted in an interview with the Guardian in April 2025.

Go back further, to a chat with French football magazine Onze Mondial in September 2023 and you get to the core of what makes Baleba tick.

In explaining his passions outside of football, Baleba talks about manga, described by the British Museum as 'Japanese comic books or graphic novels', which now has 'fans across the globe'.

His favourite series is Fist of the North Star, the hero of which is Kenshiro.…

title: Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings.

The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests.

Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn).

One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation.

"Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said.

Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta.

It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region.

The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street.

Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment.

The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear.

A humming annoyance or jobs boom? Life next to 199 data centres

AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost?

UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO.

"We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors.

He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans.

"It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC.

This kind of listing is a test of how willing companies are to keep "ploughing money" into AI, said Phillip Wool, chief research officer from Rayliant Investment Research.

Investors in Firmus would be buying into a company that is still in its early stages and is likely to need to borrow large sums of money, Wool said.

"It's more like a bet on a dream", he added.

Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment , thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability.

OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to.

There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more.

That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create .

In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public.

The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each.

AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought.

title: Sydney trader sacked for working from Singapore without permission wins unfair dismissal case
author: Nino Bucci Courts and justice reporter
text:
Employee had also been in Bali when he told his manager he was working from home, Fair Work Commission hears

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

A Sydney currency trader who was sacked for working from Singapore without approval has won an unfair dismissal case, but failed to be awarded compensation.

The Fair Work Commission ruled on Wednesday that Charles Graham had been unfairly dismissed by HIFX Australia, trading as Xe, in December last year.

Graham was sacked after his manager asked an IT worker to use his “FBI skills” and track the IP address on Graham’s laptop.

They discovered he was working from Singapore. It was also later discovered he had previously worked from Bali after telling his manager he was working from home because he had a plumber “coming around to sort out some recurring bathroom issues”.

Graham was sacked as Xe found he knew he had to get prior approval to work overseas and was to attend the office three times a week.

He said he had been holidaying in Singapore before his partner became ill with a bacterial infection, preventing him from returning to Australia.

He provided documentation, which he said showed his partner required medical treatment.

Graham had previously asked Xe if he could relocate to Singapore, but his request was denied.

Fair Work Commission commissioner Alana Matheson said that after the company sent an email to Graham advising him of its discovery on 17 November last year, the “tone … had clearly pivoted” by the following day, when he was told “there was a case to answer regarding alleged breaches of company policy”.

Over the following 10 days, a series of further email exchanges and a discussion between Xe managers took place.

Graham said in his written response to Xe that he travelled to Singapore for a holiday and that there was no relation to his previous request to relocate there, that the decision to reschedule the return flight to Australia was made over a weekend, and that as there was no expectation or precedent that he contacted his manager outside business hours, he could not inform them of this.

He said that when he did log on from Singapore rather than in Australia “he was bombarded with triaging hundreds of unread emails from his time off, fielding inbound calls and dealing with an eligible complaint from a high-value client”, and this took priority over telling his manager he was stuck overseas.

Among his other responses was that he only intended to spend a short amount of time overseas, he had not been told about specific policies regarding hybrid work, and that he had intended to let his manager know he was overseas as soon as practicable.

The company was not swayed and on 2 December last year sent him a termination letter that stated it had carefully reviewed his written submissions and found that he had not provided flight screenshots with his name, medical evidence that showed his partner was unable to travel, an adequate explanation for not telling his manager he was in Singapore, and had previously complied with “absence and approval processes”, demonstrating that he was familiar with them and had instead made “a conscious choice not to follow” them.

“Your conduct represents a serious breach of company policy, a failure to follow lawful and reasonable instructions, and an irreparable breakdown of trust and confidence,” it said in the letter.

Graham told the commission he worked remotely twice before November 2025: the previous year from Townsville, and in April and May 2025 from Bali. He had been employed by Xe for 20 months.

But his manager said she had not been aware he had ever worked remotely from overseas.

A Microsoft Teams message from Graham to his manager was included in evidence before the commission that detailed his claim he was working from home as he had a plumbing issue during one of the days he also told the commission he worked from Bali.

Matheson found that she was satisfied that the dismissal of Graham was unreasonable because while there was a valid reason for his dismissal, the process followed was procedurally unfair.

This was because Xe failed to fully raise the matters it was relying on in making the decision to dismiss Graham, Matheson said.

She found that reinstatement was inappropriate but also decided against awarding compensation.

This was, she said, in part because his misconduct contributed to the decision to dismiss him, and he was paid four weeks in lieu of notice.

title: Contribution of high value residents discussed
text:
More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy.

Jersey's high value residency programme , external grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals.

One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island.

However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling".

About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme.

O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation , external to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes.

"They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals.

"So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy."

High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income , external .

They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax , external .

O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way.

"First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income.

"And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand.

"High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off."

Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them.

He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy.

"If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said.

"So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%.

"We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax.

"We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions."

John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme.

He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly".

"I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community.

"As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all.

"I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally.

"And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work.

"They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses."

title: 'You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world'
text:
A British carmaker has unveiled plans to start production of its hand-built electric sports car in Warwickshire.

Longbow is to start production of its limited-edition Speedster at Mira Tech Park in Nuneaton next year.

West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, who backed Longbow with £3m from a government fund, said the project will be followed by the firm's Roadster model, creating more than 200 skilled jobs.

Daniel Davey, Longbow's co-chief executive officer, said the region was the best place to build the cars. "It's not just the supply chain; you've got the talent here and the know-how," he said.

Davey said: "You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world. And if you did, you would be importing UK components to it.

"So you can get heavy components elsewhere, and you can get high-volume components elsewhere; what we're looking for is low-volume, high-quality, low-cost, low-weight."

The Speedster has a waiting list of prospective buyers from across the world, waiting to spend around £85,000 on the sports car.

At the test track at Mira, the all-British creation silently demonstrated how a lightweight sports car can go from an idea to a vehicle in less than two years, helped by regional expertise.

Longbow said the UK was good at building lightweight sports cars.

"Our designers are just up the road in Leamington Spa, engineers from across the West Midlands and further afield," Davey added.

The project was backed by £3m from the government's £50m West Midlands Supplier Readiness and Transformation fund , external , which aims to accelerate the UK's transition to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the £3m was to strengthen the supply chain and the industry.

West Midlands Combined Authority said the money would be match-funded by Longbow, which plans to manufacture more than 10,000 cars a year.

Parker said: "We've been building cars here in West Midlands for 130 years, so what better location for a new generation of carmakers like Longbow.

"They know this industry inside out and are investing here because this is quite simply the best place in the UK to build a car."

Car industry expert Professor David Bailey said: "They're trying to do what Tesla first did many years ago with a sort of lightweight, fast electric sports car.

"So I think it's great; it shows we have great research and development skills. We can probably compete, I think, in terms of low-volume, high-margin cars, but more broadly we need to be doing a lot more to support the auto industry in the region and enable it to continue growing."

title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown
author: Gordon Brown
text:
We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

The coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
author: Saher Ahmed in Cairo
text:
Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood

Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood .

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.

One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.

“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.

In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Journalists’ Syndicate, whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.

Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.

For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

title: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find
author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
text:
Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it

A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.

But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.

Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet.

Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia.

Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica.

However, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River.

He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself.

Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest.

They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies.

“It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,” Magdalena said. “Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping.

“Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,” he said. “It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.”

The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journal Phytotaxa confirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies.

Harris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was “incredible”.

“I was just so excited, absolutely elated,” he said.

Magdalena said: “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.”

The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction.

Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as “large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.”

The team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature ( IUCN ) Red List designation.

Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown at Kew Gardens .

title: Three course features that could be make or break at the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
The course for the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup, Western Australia, is carved out of a landscape that delivers so many options for a gravel race and the SEVEN UCI Gravel World Series event has, over the years, tried and tested a number of them. The outcome as the organisers now deliver the rainbow jersey race is an unrelenting 144km course for the elite men and a 125.6km route for the elite women.

It will be a test with 3,179 metres of vertical gain for the women and 3,713 metres for the men on what are described as 'Liège–Bastogne–Liège climbs' as the course winds its way through the course in the Blackwood Valley. 'Draining' seems to be the word riders keep using when asked how the course is after they've had a chance to ride it for the first time.

It's the type of route where it's hard to say there are any easy portions, given there is at least 84% gravel , often long undulating plateau sections once a climb is completed and then descents where riders need to keep their wits about them so they don't slip out on the pea gravel corners. Plus it's unrelenting right to the finish.

There are, however some patches which stand out, from sections that could split the field early or create the opportunity for a final winning move, so now it's time to take a closer look at those.

Brockman – First shots fired

This isn't the first climb of the race, that honour goes to Killarney at just over 15km in, but at just 1km long with a 7.6% average the history of SEVEN has shown that it's the climb coming at around 27km into the day of racing that will start to make the difference. It's usually where the first major selection is made.

"You are going to see if you've either got good legs or bad legs on Brockman," said race director Stephen Gallagher.

The 2.4km Brockman ascent has an average gradient of 8.2% and what's more the terrain that comes after is enough for riders to dig in and try to hold on to any advantage that they reap. There is a descent off the top, but not a long one, and then the profile just plots a jagged course for the next 20km, pulling in the climbs of Adina. The real stretch of descending only comes at over the 50km mark, before a flattish section of around 10km that offers some repreive before the climbing begins all over again.

Ellis Creek – The fatigue finder

The climbs continue, and so does the wear and tear which is perhaps why Ellis Creek's 2km, 9.1% average with 169 vertical metres gain hits so hard. The challenging climb that also delivers an extra bit of steepness near the top – comes just after 85k of racing for the men and at around 65km for the women. Plus there is no real relief once you make it over the top.

"I think you've just got fatigue in the legs by that point, so that's why it's the hardest and I think it's deep enough into the race where you can go from there to the finish line," said Tasman Nankervis, the 2023 winner of the elite men's race at SEVEN who also raced this year at the UCI Gravel World Series event which replicated much of the World Championship route.

"The year I won it, I broke away from there," he said referring to the Ellis climb. "It's logical to make a move from there, whereas to make a move from Brockman, that's a bit of a high risk manoeuvre. It can be done, but you can win the race from Ellis, so I think people tend to go more in from there."

The Folly climb is a new introduction for this year, part of the finishing loop which will take the riders close to the start line but then send them off for more, including the 2.4km effort with a 4.8% average gradient that is Folly. It's bound to be packed with spectators, as it is just a short walk from the start/finish line and comes at a point where there is just over 20m of racing remaining.

It starts with riders turning on to a short but relatively steep bitumen section and then it's another turn onto the dirt, which, after a little recent rain is nicely packed down and while there are a few small rocks strewn around and some ruts in some patches they are easily avoidable as it is wide and the main line is smooth.

There is a reprieve part way through the climb which opens up to views of the rolling farmland hills, but then it just kicks in again.

Nankervis warns that this climb isn't one to be taken lightly, with a need to have something in reserve, recounting that in his race at SEVEN this year a puncture had left him behind but he made up around ten positions in this sector as it was one where the lights went out for many.

"It's really hard," added race director Gallagher. "It gets quite steep at the top. You can potentially go solo from that point if you're really strong, or you can certainly reduce a group to one or two riders."

Then before riders hit the line there are still a couple of nasty pinches and the more gradual Lindsay climb on one last descent before the winner of the rainbow jersey is decided.

title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
text:
Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.

The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.

The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.

The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday.

In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.

The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.

White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.

It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.

This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.

The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".

Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.

Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.

In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.

A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.

In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.

White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.

In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ party accuses government of mass detention of members ahead of weekend protest
author: Guardian staff and agencies
text:
Thousands expected to march in Delhi on Saturday, as anger mounts over controversial changes to voter lists in world’s largest democracy

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.

Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of ⁠voter lists .

Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.

A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.

Police authorities ⁠didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.

The CJP said that ‌among those detained was a group ‌of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being ‌taken away in a bus to an unknown location.

The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.

The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.

The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.

The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.

The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the ​resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks .

In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.

Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.

“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who ⁠actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture ​student who attended the Bengaluru protest.

There were also protests over ​police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.

On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of ​using “brute force” to briefly detain ‌party leader Rahul Gandhi, his ​sister Priyanka Vadra, and other ​lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.

Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.

BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.

Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

title: New Delhi Deploys Heavy Security Ahead of Voter-Roll Protest
author: Rajesh Roy and Sudhi Ranjan Sen
text: From mass detentions to liquor-store closures, authorities in New Delhi are leaving little to chance as they prepare for a weekend of protests over a contentious revision of India’s voter rolls.
